tool.heroSubtitle: Every named divine being in Scripture, what the text calls it, and what the ancient world thought it was.

footer.text: The method. Every occurrence count here comes from the interlinear index rather than a commentary, so a number can be checked against the text itself. Everything written is cited to the Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible, to Heiser, Walton, or to Smith's Baal Cycle commentary, and where a reading is disputed the entry says so instead of picking a side quietly.

entries.title: Yahweh
entries.summary: The personal name of Israel's God, printed as LORD in most English Bibles.
entries.strong: H3068 (יהוה), 6,513 occ; H3069 (יֱהוִה, the same name pointed with the vowels of *elohim*), 315 occ; 6,828 together, which is the standard count
entries.note: The personal name of Israel's God. Almost every English Bible prints LORD in small capitals in its place. The substitution is a Jewish reverence practice that Christian translation carried over, and it says nothing about what the name means. The name is unattested anywhere in the ancient Near East before 1200 BC, and DDD traces the cult south of Israel, to Edom, Seir, and Midian, rather than to Canaan. Two Egyptian topographical lists, one from the reign of Amenophis III and one from Ramesses II, place "Yahu in the land of the Shasu-bedouin" in that same country, and the biblical theophany texts agree with them: Judges 5:4 and Deuteronomy 33:2 both have Yahweh coming from Seir and Paran.
entries.dissent: Whether the name is a causative form of the verb "to be" is disputed, and Exodus 3:14 is a hard verse to render. Even granting a verbal origin, scholars split between a simple Qal reading ("he is, he shows himself") and a causative Hiphil ("he causes to be, brings into existence"). Knauf argues instead from the Arabic root *hwy*, "to blow," which would make Yahweh a storm god in origin, and DDD calls that the more plausible reading given where the name comes from. Some of the storm imagery belongs to Yahweh outright and runs alongside the monarchic Baal cult rather than after it: the chariot of clouds, the lightning-voice, Zion cast as "the recesses of Zaphon" (Psalm 48:2-3). DDD also puts a limit on the southern-origin story. It keeps the Kenite hypothesis only in a modified form, faults the classical version for ignoring Israel's Canaanite roots and leaning on a historically problematic Moses, and places the handoff inside Palestine, with Kenite or Midianite traders on the caravan routes, instead of on a desert march.
sources: LSB preface on the divine name

entries.title: El
entries.summary: The ordinary word for god in the region, and also the name of the chief god of Israel's neighbors.
entries.note: The generic West Semitic word for god, and also the proper name of the head of the Ugaritic pantheon. Israel used it of Yahweh without apology (Genesis 33:20). DDD lists a cluster of other El names with a Canaanite background still visible in the Hebrew: *el berit* (Judges 9:46), *el olam* (Genesis 21:33), *el elyon* (Genesis 14:18-22), *el roi* (Genesis 16:13), and *el shadday*. When the king of Tyre claims a divine seat "in the heart of the seas" in Ezekiel 28:2, he is borrowing the same Ugaritic geography as El's own dwelling at "the fountainhead of the two rivers."
entries.ane: El at Ugarit is the aged father of the gods who presides over the assembly, and the biblical writers take his vocabulary while refusing his mythology. Ugaritic texts call him "the benevolent, good-natured El" (*ltpn il dpid*), describe the grey hair of his beard, and give him the epithet *tr*, "bull," for his strength and dignity. Israel keeps the aged, bearded image and hangs it on Yahweh: Daniel's Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9) is El's beard on Yahweh's frame.

entries.title: El Elyon
entries.summary: A title meaning Most High, used in the verse where the nations get handed out to different gods.
entries.note: Most High. In Deuteronomy 32:8 Elyon divides the nations and assigns them, and what he assigns them to is where the divine council framework begins. The Masoretic Text ends verse 8 with "according to the number of the sons of Israel," but the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read "sons of God," and nearly every modern critical edition follows them. The scrolls give two witnesses rather than one: 4QDeutj reads *bny 'lhym*, "sons of God," while 4QDeutq has room for more consonants after the *'l*, pointing to "sons of El" or "sons of the gods." The Masoretic reading can't be original anyway, since the Babel dispersal the verse describes happens generations before Israel exists as a people. Deuteronomy 4:19-20 is the companion text, where Yahweh "allotted" the other nations their gods the same way he "took" Israel as his own portion.
entries.dissent: Whether Elyon and Yahweh are one figure or two in Deuteronomy 32:8-9 is a real argument, and DDD argues it both ways in two different articles. Its Elyon article reads the *ki* of verse 9 as asseverative ("Indeed, Yahweh's own portion was his people"), which makes the dividing and the portion-taking one act and Elyon an epithet for Yahweh. Parker's "Sons of (the) God(s)" article has Elyon as the old high god handing out the territories, with Yahweh receiving Israel at his hands. Verse 9 is where it is decided.
sources: Heiser, "Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God," *Bibliotheca Sacra* 158
S. B. Parker, DDD s.v. "Sons of (the) God(s)," 794-799

entries.title: El Shaddai
entries.summary: An old title for Israel's God, translated Almighty, whose actual meaning is disputed.
entries.note: Rendered "Almighty" on the strength of the Septuagint, which uses *pantokrator* throughout Job, and not on the strength of the Hebrew. Two real etymologies compete. The older one derives Shadday from Akkadian *shadu*, "mountain" (Albright, Cross); Knauf argues for a root tied to Akkadian *shadi* and Hebrew *sadeh*, "the uncultivated wilderness," which makes El Shadday a god of the wild country and fits the iconography of a lord of wild animals. DDD treats "breast" as no etymology at all, only a pun the text makes in Genesis 49:25, where Shadday sits beside "blessings of breasts and womb." Walton reads Abraham's devotion to El Shadday through the Mesopotamian pattern of a personal god, a patron attached to an individual or a clan rather than a whole people, which fits the Priestly claim in Exodus 6:3 that the patriarchs knew God by this name before Yahweh was revealed.
entries.invented: The devotional gloss "the God of more than enough" has no lexical basis.
sources: Walton, *Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament*, ch. 6 ("State and Family Religion")

entries.title: Yahweh Tzevaot
entries.summary: A battle title: the God of armies, meaning heavenly ones rather than Israel's soldiers.
entries.strong: H6635 (צָבָא), 486 occ of the noun, in 463 verses
entries.note: Yahweh of armies, and the armies aren't Israel's infantry. The title puts him at the head of the heavenly host. It gathers in throne-room scenes. DDD counts 284 uses as a divine name, 121 of them free rather than formulaic, though DDD isn't consistent on this: its Archon article gives the figure as some 267. The uses concentrate in Isaiah 1-39, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, texts tied to the Jerusalem temple's own theology, and the title is nearly absent from the Pentateuch and Ezekiel. Its older, fuller form is the cherubim formula, "Yahweh Zebaoth, enthroned on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2; Isaiah 37:16), and that formula describes the Solomonic temple's actual furniture: two cherubim forming an empty throne, with the ark for a footstool. The LXX renders the title three ways depending on the book, most often *pantokrator*, "Almighty," sometimes a transliterated "Sabaoth," and sometimes "Lord of Powers."
sources: DDD s.v. "Yahweh Zebaoth," 920-921 (the 284 and 121 figures open the article)

entries.title: The Angel of Yahweh
entries.summary: A messenger who shows up speaking as God himself, and gets treated as God by the people who meet him.
entries.note: Speaks as Yahweh in the first person, accepts worship, is called Yahweh by the narrator, and is still distinct enough from Yahweh to be sent by him. The tension sits in the text before any theology gets built on it. Exodus 23:21 gives the mechanism: Israel is to obey this angel because "my name is in him," which Heiser reads as the angel carrying Yahweh's own presence instead of working as an ordinary messenger. In Numbers 22:22-35 the figure stands in the road with a drawn sword and speaks on his own authority ("I have come out as an adversary"), never claiming to relay someone else's words, and in 2 Samuel 24:16 he is the one Yahweh personally calls off after striking Jerusalem ("Enough, now relax your hand"). Judges 13 makes the identification from the human side. After the Angel rises in the flame of Manoah's sacrifice, Manoah tells his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God," the conviction behind Exodus 33:20's "man shall not see me and live," and his wife reasons from the accepted sacrifice back to their safety without ever correcting the claim that they saw God. Nobody in the episode, the narrator included, draws the line between the Angel and God that later theology sometimes wants drawn.
entries.dissent: The two-powers reading and the plain-messenger reading both have serious defenders. One resolution has the Angel carrying Yahweh's Presence and Name without being Yahweh in his totality, a distinct personage bearing the Name rather than a second deity. DDD goes the other way. Where the identity wavers across the Hebrew, LXX and Vulgate, it concludes the instability is best resolved by the interpolation theory: later scribes, uncomfortable with God appearing directly, inserted *mal'ak* into texts that were originally straightforward Yahweh theophanies (Genesis 16, Judges 6, and Exodus 4:24, where the insertion is undeniable because some witnesses lack it). DDD rejects the preincarnate-Christ identification as against the authors' intent, rejects theophany and hypostasis readings because *mal'ak* has to mean a subordinate, and calls the idea that a messenger's identity could merge with his sender's simply incorrect.
sources: Speliopoulos & Mangum, "Angel of Yahweh," *Lexham Bible Dictionary*
Keil and Delitzsch, *Commentary on the Old Testament*, 1:119 (on Judges 13:19-23)

entries.title: The Commander of Yahweh's Army
entries.summary: An armed figure who meets Joshua outside Jericho and refuses to take a side.
entries.note: Answers Joshua's "are you for us or for them" with "no." He tells Joshua to take off his sandals, the signal from Exodus 3, and Joshua worships him without being corrected.
entries.dissent: Identifying him with the Angel of Yahweh is common, and the text doesn't require it. Unlike the angels who refuse worship elsewhere in Scripture, this figure bears God's name and lets Joshua's worship stand, and the sandal command invites the comparison with the burning bush on purpose. Heiser adds a textual argument: the Hebrew Bible puts a drawn sword in a heavenly figure's hand in only two other places, Numbers 22:23 and 1 Chronicles 21:16, and both of those figures are named as the Angel of Yahweh. DDD's "Host of Heaven" article separately flags Joshua 5:13-15 as one of the few surviving glimpses of the older, military sense of the host of heaven, the armed divine retinue behind the tamer later picture of angels praising God around a throne (1 Kings 22:19).

entries.title: The Son of Man
entries.summary: A human-looking figure in Daniel's vision who arrives on the clouds and is handed authority over everything.
entries.note: A figure who rides the clouds, which every other time in the Hebrew Bible is something only Yahweh does, and who receives dominion from the Ancient of Days. Jesus claims it at his trial and the claim produces the blasphemy charge. DDD takes Daniel 7:13-14 as the earliest text for the non-generic sense: an ordinary Semitic idiom for a human being becomes a heavenly figure in the Jewish texts, and then Jesus in the New Testament. Walton flags the Mesopotamian Anzu myth as possible background for the beast imagery of Daniel 7 in general, a narrower and more cautious claim than an explanation of the Son of Man himself.
sources: Walton, "The Anzu Myth as Relevant Background for Daniel 7?" in *The Book of Daniel: Composition and Reception* (2001) ---

entries.title: Bene elohim
entries.summary: Sons of God: a group of lesser divine beings who show up at God's throne.
entries.note: Sons of God. Plural, created, subordinate, and present at the throne. The phrase doesn't mean "angels" in the later systematic sense, and it doesn't mean human worshippers. DDD's Parker treats it as an idiom for "divine beings" on the model of *bene ha-adam*, "human beings." Hebrew grammar leaves it open whether the second noun in the phrase is singular or plural, and when the LXX flattens both *elohim* and *elim* to *theou*, that is one resolution of the ambiguity rather than the only one an ancient reader had. Yahweh's first-person plurals read the same way: in Genesis 1:26 ("let us make") and 3:22 ("like one of us") a human is compared to one of a group of divine beings among whom Yahweh is first. Isaiah 6:8's "who will go for us" belongs to the same pattern, now inside an explicit council scene. Parker also reads Deuteronomy 32:8 with Elyon as a high god distinct from Yahweh, which DDD's own Elyon article disputes; see the El Elyon dissent.
entries.ane: The Ugaritic *'dt 'ilm*, "assembly of El" or "assembly of the gods," is the closest parallel to the council language of Psalm 82:1, and it is the same phrase rather than a similar idea. Ugaritic *bn il* ("sons of El") and *bn ilm* ("sons of the gods") name the same group and are swapped freely in the Ugaritic texts, the direct linguistic parallel to the Hebrew wavering between *bene elohim* and *bene elim*. Both traditions used the phrase to mean "the gods" without stopping to ask whether the second noun was technically singular or plural.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 6-11 reads Genesis 6 this way, and so does Jubilees 5. Daniel 3:25 gives the Aramaic singular of the same phrase, *bar-elahin*, "a son of the gods," for the fourth figure in the furnace, and Nebuchadnezzar's own explanation in 3:28 calls him Yahweh's messenger, so the older divine-plural language is already being absorbed into the newer and more monotheistic word "angel."
entries.dissent: The Sethite reading of Genesis 6 has a long pedigree and a weak textual base.
sources: S. B. Parker, DDD s.v. "Sons of (the) God(s)," 794-799
Heiser, "Divine Council," in *Dictionary of the Old Testament: Wisdom, Poetry & Writings* (IVP Academic, 2008), 113

entries.title: The elohim of Psalm 82
entries.summary: A psalm where God stands up in a room full of gods and sentences them to death.
entries.note: God stands in the assembly of El and judges among the *elohim*. A singular *elohim* judges plural *elohim* in the same breath, and the human-judges reading has to work hard to get around it. DDD's Parker reads the psalm as a courtroom scene aimed at exposing the gods' failure: Yahweh charges them with corrupt government (vv. 2-4), they have no answer, and the closing verse acclaims Yahweh as their successor and heir to the nations they mismanaged. The move only works if verse 6's "gods, sons of Elyon" are real members of the court. Yahweh is made to say he once shared the ordinary belief that they were gods, so that he can now announce their mortality and their end.
entries.ane: DDD's Lelli notes that Psalm 89:6-9, which praises Yahweh as one god among "the sons of the mighty" and "the council of the holy ones," and Job 15:15, where even the holy ones aren't trusted and the heavens aren't clean in God's eyes, both assume what Psalm 82 assumes: a heavenly council of lesser *elohim*, older than Israel's own monotheistic sharpening of the language.
entries.dissent: The human-judges reading is the majority view in older commentaries and still has defenders. Verse 7, "you shall die like men," is its strongest card and also its weakest.
sources: S. B. Parker, DDD s.v. "Sons of (the) God(s)," 794-799 §III on Psalm 82
F. Lelli, DDD s.v. "Stars," 810-814 (on Psalm 89's council of the holy ones and Job 15:15)

entries.title: The host of heaven
entries.summary: Two things at once: God's heavenly army, and the sun, moon and stars Israel was told not to worship.
entries.note: Two uses that sit uneasily together, the army standing around Yahweh's throne and the astral bodies Israel is forbidden to worship. Deuteronomy 4:19 turns the second into an allotment, the same move as 32:8. Niehr reads the two senses as one history: the army comes first, the stars arrive under Mesopotamian influence in the eighth and seventh centuries, and the Deuteronomists strip the astral sense back out.
sources: H. Niehr, DDD s.v. "Host of Heaven," 428-429

entries.title: Seraphim
entries.summary: Six-winged beings around God's throne in Isaiah's vision, described with a word that elsewhere means burning serpent.
entries.note: The same word names the burning serpents in the wilderness and the throne attendants of Isaiah 6, and five of its seven occurrences are serpents. The iconography behind it is the winged uraeus, not a chubby European angel. DDD's Mettinger puts a limit on the parallel: Judahite seals of the period show two-winged and four-winged uraei, but a six-winged uraeus, Isaiah's count, isn't attested anywhere in the iconographic record, so the match between text and image is close without being exact. Isaiah also turns the motif around. Elsewhere the uraeus protects the god or king it guards, while in Isaiah 6 the seraphim cover themselves with their wings before a Yahweh who needs no protecting. The antiphonal "holy, holy, holy" of verse 3 means there are at least two of them.
entries.ane: The winged cobra is standard Egyptian royal-guardian imagery in the period, and royal Judahite seals carrying Israelite names show four-winged uraei in the eighth century BC, so Isaiah's audience already knew the picture. The uraeus's Egyptian name means "flame," which lines up with *saraph*'s "burning" better than a literal-fire reading does, since cobra venom causes the searing pain the word describes elsewhere.

entries.title: Cherubim
entries.summary: Winged composite creatures that guard and carry God's throne, nothing like the babies in later art.
entries.note: Throne guardians and throne bearers, composite creatures with four faces in Ezekiel, stationed at the entrance to sacred space with a flaming sword. Mettinger, who wrote the DDD entry, separates two iconographic programs the Bible keeps apart: the Solomonic cherubim, ten cubits high, standing side by side with their wings joined to form the throne seat itself (1 Kings 6:23-27), and the Priestly tabernacle cherubim, small, facing each other, and hammered out of one piece with the ark's lid (Exodus 25:19-20). The epithet "he who is enthroned on the cherubim" (*yoshev ha-keruvim*) is already attached to Yahweh at Shiloh (1 Samuel 4:4) and recurs at 2 Samuel 6:2 and Isaiah 37:16. Ezekiel's cherubim turn the static throne into a mobile throne-chariot, and Psalm 18:10's Yahweh "riding on a cherub" comes from the same tradition, which Mettinger ties to an exilic need for a God whose presence could travel with a displaced people.
entries.ane: The lamassu and the sphinx-throne of Syro-Palestinian kings are the direct visual parallel, a king enthroned on winged composite beasts. The sphinx-throne is itself a Syrian development out of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty and was used for gods and kings alike, unlike Egypt's own lion-paw throne, which never carried a deity. A Late Bronze Age ivory plaque from Megiddo shows a king on a throne of winged sphinxes, and so does the tenth-century relief on the Ahiram sarcophagus. The empty cherubim throne of the Solomonic temple, standing over the ark as an invisible deity's footstool (1 Kings 8:6-8), belongs to Israelite aniconism: it combines two aniconic traditions, the empty throne and the ark, where Phoenician and Punic art seats Baal Hammon and Astarte on comparable sphinx thrones in plain view.
entries.invented: The Renaissance putto. There is no biblical basis for the baby.
sources: Walton, *Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary: 1 & 2 Kings...*, 192
Walton, *Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament*

entries.title: Ophanim
entries.summary: The wheels full of eyes in Ezekiel's vision, which later tradition turned into a class of angel.
entries.strong: H212 (אוֹפָן), 35 occ (a common noun for "wheel"; 25 of the 35 are in Ezekiel, and the rest are ordinary chariot and potter's wheels)
entries.note: Wheels full of eyes that move with the living creatures and have the spirit of the creatures in them. Whether they are beings or throne machinery is unclear in Ezekiel and only gets settled in later tradition.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 71:7 lists ophanim with cherubim and seraphim as a class of being ("the sleepless ones who guard the throne of his glory"), a later development and not Ezekiel's own framing.
sources: Faithlife Study Bible on Ezekiel 1. DDD has no article for ophanim, only a bare cross-reference to "Angels" (648), and the wheels are under-theorized in the academic literature as well.

entries.title: The Watchers of Daniel 4
entries.summary: Heavenly figures in one chapter of Daniel who announce a king's downfall.
entries.note: Three occurrences, all in one chapter, all in Aramaic, always paired with "holy one," and always issuing a decree against a king. This is the only canonical use of the term and it is neutral; the Watchers here have not fallen. The Aramaic *'ir* likely comes from the verb "to be awake," a watcher being one who stays awake, which suits an angelic sentinel, and the "holy" in verse 13 marks this one as God's own rather than a rebel. DDD's Collins traces two paths for the word after Daniel. Alongside the fallen Watchers of 1 Enoch, it keeps its neutral sense in other Second Temple texts, for instance the four archangels "who watch" or "who sleep not" at 1 Enoch 20:1 and the "Watchers and holy ones" of 3 Enoch 28, both drawing on Daniel 4 directly rather than on the fallen-angel tradition. The nearest biblical precedent for the idea, though not the word, is Psalm 121:4, "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep."
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 6-16 uses the same title for the beings who descend on Hermon, and the negative sense comes from there. Collins finds two strands inside that Enochic material. One names the leader Shemihazah and puts the sin in illicit marriage with human women; the other names him Asael or Azazel and puts the sin in illicit teaching (astrology, metallurgy, cosmetics, spells). 1 Enoch as it stands combines both. The Damascus Document (CD 2:18) speaks of "the fall of the Watchers of heaven," and the Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen 2:1,16) ties the Watchers to the Nephilim and "the sons of heaven" around the birth of Noah. Heiser's *Reversing Hermon* argues that this Watcher tradition, more than Genesis 3 alone, is the New Testament's default explanation for how thoroughly corrupt humanity became, and that undoing what happened on Hermon frames the mission of Jesus across several NT texts.

entries.title: The morning stars
entries.summary: Stars that sing at the creation of the world, set in parallel with the sons of God.
entries.note: Set in parallel with "all the sons of God," and Hebrew poetry puts equivalents in the B-line, so the morning stars are a class of being and not lights. They shout at the founding of the earth, so they predate it. Lelli's entry on Stars reads the joy of the stars there alongside Job 15:15's "he does not trust his holy ones" and Job 25:5, where even the moon and stars are unclean in God's eyes. All three assume a divine entourage that is subordinate to Yahweh and corruptible before him, with the stars as its visible members.
entries.secondTemple: 11QTargum of Job renders Job 38:7 as "when the morning stars shone together and all the angels of God shouted together," replacing the parallel *bene elohim* clause with "angels" outright. It is the earliest datable Jewish reading of the verse, and it already takes the morning stars as divine beings while quietly closing off any polytheistic reading of the older Hebrew.
sources: F. Lelli, DDD s.v. "Stars," 810-814 (DDD has no "Morning Star" headword

entries.title: Michael
entries.summary: The angel assigned to Israel, and the only figure the Bible calls an archangel.
entries.strong: H4317, G3413; the entities record carries 15 refs (13 Hebrew, 2 Greek), most of them human namesakes, refs (the being): Daniel 10:13,21; Daniel 12:1; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7
entries.note: Called one of the chief princes and "your prince," Israel's assigned *sar*, the counterpart to the princes of Persia and Greece. The geopolitics of Daniel 10 are cosmic before they are military. DDD's Mach warns that Michael grew so prominent in Second Temple Judaism that later writers pulled almost any unnamed biblical angel into his orbit, so traditions originally about Michael need separating from generic angel traditions attached to him afterward. His usual Second Temple title, *archistrategos*, "chief commander," most likely translates "commander of the LORD's army" from Joshua 5:14, though that verse never names him.
entries.secondTemple: The oldest surviving list of archangels puts Michael first among four (1 Enoch 9-10, with Gabriel, Raphael, and Uriel or Sariel), and the group grows to seven in 1 Enoch 20. In 3 Baruch 11-15 he is the sole mediator between God and the guardian angels of individual nations, receiving their prayers. Jude 9's dispute with the devil over Moses' body draws on the lost Assumption of Moses, and the Life of Adam and Eve (Vita 13-14) supplies the earliest surviving version of Michael as Satan's direct opponent, tied there to a refusal to worship Adam.
entries.dissent: Jude 9 depends on a lost work, probably the Assumption of Moses, and some readers treat that as disqualifying.
entries.invented: The Jehovah's Witness identification of Michael with the pre-incarnate Christ rests on "the voice of the archangel" in 1 Thessalonians 4:16, which is a comparison and not an equation.
sources: Heiser, *Unseen Realm*, ch. 15, note-to-build: existing record is `kind: person` and uncurated
split the being from the human Michaels

entries.title: Gabriel
entries.summary: The angel who explains visions and announces births, named four times in the Bible.
entries.note: Named four times, twice to Daniel and twice in Luke's opening chapter, and he interprets and announces. Scripture never calls him an archangel. DDD's Collins prefers "God is my hero" or "my warrior" to the more common "man of God" for the name, arguing from Eblaite personal names, and Daniel's "the man Gabriel" (8:15; 9:21) is likely a play on the *gever*, "man," inside the name. Gabriel and Michael are the only two angels named in the Hebrew Bible; Raphael is the third named angel in the wider canon, in Tobit.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 9-10 gives him a standing role among the four who intercede. He appears in the oldest four-archangel list (1 Enoch 9:1, with Michael, Raphael, and Sariel) and in the seven of 1 Enoch 20 (with Uriel, Raphael, Raguel, Michael, Sariel, and Remiel). In 2 Enoch 24:1 he sits at God's left hand, and Aramaic incantation bowls from Babylonia sometimes invoke his name ahead of Michael's. The Targumim later credit him with leading Joseph to his brothers (on Genesis 37:15), helping Michael bury Moses (on Deuteronomy 34:6), and destroying Sennacherib's army (on 2 Chronicles 32:21).
sources: J. J. Collins, DDD s.v. "Gabriel," 338, note-to-build: already `curated: true` in entities.json

entries.title: The princes of Persia and Greece
entries.summary: Spirit figures in Daniel who rule nations and can hold up a messenger from God for weeks.
entries.note: A messenger is held up twenty-one days by the prince of Persia, needs Michael's help to get through, and warns that the prince of Greece comes next. The nations have beings set over them, and those beings resist. Heiser argues the princes of Daniel 10 are the real background for Paul's language of hostile cosmic authorities: the Septuagint and Theodotion both render the Hebrew *sar* as *archon*, and *archon*, with cognates like *arche* and *exousia*, is the vocabulary Paul uses for "the rulers of this age" (1 Corinthians 2:6,8), "the rulers in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 3:10), and "the ruler of the power of the air" (Ephesians 2:2). Scholars agree the idea in Daniel 10 goes back to Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where Elyon divided the nations among the sons of God at Babel (in the Qumran and LXX text) and kept Israel for himself. Paul's reasoning for the mission in Acts 17:26-27, that God set the nations' boundaries so they would seek him and find him, reads as a direct answer to that arrangement, with the disinherited nations to be reclaimed and not merely individuals converted.
sources: Clifford, "History and Myth in Daniel 10-12," BASOR
Ronn Johnson, "The Old Testament Background for Paul's Principalities and Powers," PhD diss., DTS, 2004

entries.title: The satan of Job
entries.summary: The accuser in Job, a job title in God's court rather than a personal name.
entries.strong: H7854 (שָׂטָן), 27 occ in 23 verses. DDD's count of nine is a count of passages, not words: the noun turns up in nine contexts, five where the satan is human and four where it is celestial (Numbers 22, Job 1-2, Zechariah 3, 1 Chronicles 21). Job 1-2 alone accounts for fourteen of the 27 tokens.
entries.note: Carries the definite article in Job and Zechariah, *ha-satan*, "the adversary," a role in the court rather than a personal name. In Numbers 22 the word describes the Angel of Yahweh himself doing the job. DDD's Day, working through all four celestial passages, argues that the article makes a proper-name reading grammatically very unlikely and that "the Accuser" as a fixed office in the divine council has no convincing legal parallel in Israel or the wider ancient Near East; the nearest analogues are Akkadian *bel dababi* and *bel dini*, "legal opponent," which describe a function and not a title. Her alternative is that the article marks a temporary status, as in Genesis 14:13's "the fugitive," so that any of several council members could act as a satan on a given occasion. On that reading the satan of Numbers 22, Yahweh's own messenger sent to stop Balaam, and the satan of Zechariah 3, arguing against Joshua and opposed by Yahweh's messenger, need not be the same figure at all. Heiser makes the same point from the count: most of the 27 occurrences carry the article, and neither Hebrew nor English puts a definite article on a personal name.
entries.dissent: Whether 1 Chronicles 21:1, which drops the article, is the first use of *satan* as a name is argued both ways. The only other place an anarthrous *satan* names a divine figure is Numbers 22:22, where the Angel of Yahweh is called "a satan," and since God and the Angel are repeatedly identified elsewhere, one resolution reads 1 Chronicles 21:1 as the Angel acting as adversary, Yahweh in Angel-form, which would mean Chronicles and 2 Samuel 24:1 were never in tension. Heiser argues exactly this: Numbers 22:22 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 are the only two places an anarthrous *satan* names a divine rather than a human adversary, and since Numbers identifies its *satan* as the Angel of Yahweh, and God and the Angel are repeatedly identified with each other, the Chronicler's *satan* is the Angel dispensing God's judgment rather than a cosmic enemy. On his count ten of the 27 occurrences lack the article, and even those need not name a personalized figure, since the phrase can simply mean "an adversary." Day reads the Chronicler's swap of *satan* for Yahweh's anger (2 Samuel 24:1) as a narrower concern than distancing Yahweh from evil in general, since that motive can't explain 2 Chronicles 18:18-22, where Yahweh sanctions a lying spirit outright. The Chronicler needed to protect David's reputation in a census story he couldn't delete, because it explains the founding of the temple's altar site. Even if *satan* works as a name by 1 Chronicles 21:1, it sits three centuries short of the developed New Testament devil; the earliest certain uses of Satan as a proper name are Second Temple (Assumption of Moses 10:1; Jubilees 23:29; possibly Sirach 21:27).
entries.invented: Reading Job's adversary as the fully formed devil of later Christian theology imports three centuries of development into chapter 1.
sources: C. Breytenbach and P. L. Day, "Satan," DDD, 726-731

entries.title: The lying spirit
entries.summary: A spirit who volunteers at God's throne to deceive a king's prophets.
entries.note: Micaiah sees Yahweh enthroned with the host around him. Yahweh asks for a volunteer, and a spirit steps forward with a plan to deceive Ahab's prophets, so a prophet reports a council scene, with a deliberation and an assignment, as the reason a king is about to die. McCarter treats the unnamed spirit of 1 Kings 22:21 as a rare personified, semi-independent council member, distinct from the unpersonified "evil spirit" that torments Saul (1 Samuel 16:14-23; 18:10-11; 19:9), which reads better as a psychological or narrative device than an individual being. He points to one near parallel: Eliphaz's night apparition in Job 4:12-21, a spirit with a discernible form that lectures him on the corruptibility of God's own angels without any stated divine commission.
entries.ane: McCarter cites the Mesopotamian contrast between the "good wind" (*shar tabu*) and the "evil wind" (*shar lemnu*), the latter epitomized by a standard set of seven evil spirits blamed for human misfortune, as the closest ancient Near Eastern parallel to Israel's "evil spirit from Yahweh." Micaiah's scene itself, a spirit volunteering inside a convened royal council, has no exact Mesopotamian counterpart in the sources DDD surveys.
sources: Heiser, *Unseen Realm*, on the council at work
P. K. McCarter, DDD s.v. "Evil Spirit of God," 319 (DDD's "Spirit" headword is only a cross-reference to Holy Spirit)

entries.title: The destroyer
entries.summary: The killing figure of the Passover night, later seen again with a drawn sword over Jerusalem.
entries.note: *Mashchit*, "Destroyer," a Hiphil participle of *sh-ch-t*, "ruin, mar, destroy," a root used elsewhere of cloth, pots, vineyards, and cities. It passes through Egypt, is held back by the blood, and halts at the threshing floor of Araunah, and Paul mentions it as a known figure without explaining it. DDD files it under "Destroyer," separate from the angel of death who takes individuals at their natural end, and draws the line by function: the Destroyer kills in numbers and before their time, always on Yahweh's specific order and never on its own, and is always checked by a cultic act. The fuller account in 1 Chronicles 21 gives it a visible, gigantic form with a drawn sword it sheathes when Yahweh calls it off (vv. 16, 27, 30), matching "the angel who was destroying" in 2 Samuel 24:16. Ezekiel 9 has a further scene that usually gets missed, where unnamed executioners are commissioned "to destroy" (*lemashit*, v. 6) Jerusalem's guilty and are stopped only where a mark has been set on the innocent, the same restrained slaughter as Exodus 12 and 1 Chronicles 21.
entries.secondTemple: The wilderness plague of Numbers 17 never uses *mashit*, but it was read as the Destroyer's work by the time of 1 Corinthians 10:10 ("they were destroyed by the Destroyer," with the same Greek root the LXX uses for Exodus 12 and 1 Chronicles 21) and Wisdom of Solomon 18:25, and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan writes the Aramaic equivalent of "Destroyer" straight into Numbers 17:11. Revelation 9:11 gives "Destroyer" (Apollyon) as the Greek name of the angel of the abyss, which ties the figure to Abaddon.

entries.title: Angels
entries.summary: A word that means messenger and describes a job, not a species of being.
entries.strong: H4397 (מַלְאָךְ), 213 occ (DDD counts over 200 including human messengers); G32 (ἄγγελος), 175 occ
entries.note: The word means messenger and is used of human messengers throughout. It names a job and not a species, and an angelology built on the word alone flattens the council's real variety into one category. DDD's Meier gives a concrete case: an early Israelite wouldn't have called the theriomorphic cherubim or seraphim *mal'akim*, since creatures that terrifying were unlikely carriers of a message to a human being, and in fact neither one ever delivers one in the Bible. The catch-all sense of "angel," any supernatural being under God's authority whether or not it carries a message, comes later. It is absent from D and P and from most pre-exilic prophecy, where God simply speaks, and it becomes dominant only in the Apocrypha, the NT, and the later biblical books. The LXX's choices already show discomfort with the older and plainer "sons of God": it renders Job 2:1's *bene elohim* as *angeloi theou*, and Theodotion reworks Daniel's Watcher language into angel vocabulary in the same way.
entries.secondTemple: The angel of Yahweh who strikes down Sennacherib's army (2 Kings 19:35, with parallels at Isaiah 37:36 and 2 Chronicles 32:21) becomes the model case of an angel carrying out mass, decisive judgment, and 2 Maccabees 15:22-23 cites the episode as precedent when it asks God to do it again.

entries.title: Archangel
entries.summary: A rank that appears twice in the New Testament and belongs to Michael alone.
entries.note: Twice in the whole New Testament. Michael is the only figure who gets the title, and the nine orders come from Pseudo-Dionysius in the fifth or sixth century. The figure is already in the Hebrew Bible, but the Greek word *archangelos* never appears in the Greek Old Testament. It turns up in the Pseudepigrapha, then twice here. There, the Greek title *archistrategos*, "chief commander," given to Michael in Second Temple texts (Testament of Abraham 1:4; 2 Enoch 22:6), most likely renders "commander of the LORD's host" from Joshua 5:14, even though Joshua never names its commander. The lists themselves shift. The earliest has four archangels (1 Enoch 9:1: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Sariel), a later one has seven (1 Enoch 20 adds Uriel, Raguel, and Remiel), and Uriel and Phanuel trade places as the fourth name across manuscript traditions, the same instability recorded under Uriel, Sariel, Phanuel below.
entries.invented: Seven archangels with fixed names and portfolios are Second Temple and later, not biblical.
sources: J. W. van Henten, DDD s.v. "Archangel," 80-81

entries.title: The holy ones
entries.summary: A name for the beings who make up God's court.
entries.note: *Qedoshim*. In Psalm 89 they are the assembly around Yahweh, in parallel with the *bene elim*, and in these passages the word designates the council and not Israel. DDD files the singular title and the plural council together under "Holy One" and roots both in *QDS*, "reserved for a god, sacred." Applied to Yahweh alone and without the article, *qadosh* becomes the divine epithet "the Holy One" (Isaiah 40:25; 57:15; Habakkuk 3:3; Job 6:10); in the plural without the article it becomes a name for the council, as in Hosea 12:1, Proverbs 9:10, and Proverbs 30:3, where *qedoshim* stands in parallel with El and Eloah. DDD reads the overlap as a byproduct of Yahweh's identification with El: the Holy One and his holy ones both come from the same Northwest Semitic root sense, applied at two points in the same kind of sentence.
sources: F. van Koppen & K. van der Toorn, DDD s.v. "Holy One," 415-417

entries.title: Raphael
entries.summary: An angel who works as a physician and demon-binder in Tobit, a book outside the Protestant Bible.
entries.note: Named as one of the seven who stand before the glory of the Lord. He is in the Catholic and Orthodox canons through Tobit and in 1 Enoch, and absent from the Protestant Old Testament. DDD's Mach derives the name from the root *RP'*, "to heal" (*rapha*, "physician"), so that Raphael reads "God healed," and leaves one question open: whether the name has anything to do with the Rephaim, which DDD says has not yet been studied. In Tobit he works as a physician and demon-binder more than a messenger. He prescribes the fish-gall remedy for Tobit's blindness, uses the fish's other parts to drive off and bind the demon Asmodaeus (Tobit 6:1-9; 8:3), and says outright that he never ate or drank with Tobias's family, since the shared meal was only an appearance (Tobit 12:19).
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 9-10 and 20; also 40:9 ("set over all disease and every wound of the children of the people") and 54:6, where his task is healing the earth of the Watchers' damage, including the binding of Azazel.

entries.title: Uriel, Sariel, Phanuel
entries.summary: Angels named in 1 Enoch that readers go looking for in the Bible and never find.
entries.note: Named archangels in 1 Enoch's lists, each with an assigned domain. They are in Enoch's lists and nowhere in the Bible. DDD's Mach notes that the name Uriel is itself disputed between a Hebrew root (light) and an Aramaic one (fire), and that the three names behave as interchangeable slots more than fixed individuals across the manuscripts: Phanuel replaces Uriel as the fourth archangel in the Similitudes of Enoch (1 Enoch 37-71), and elsewhere Uriel and Sariel swap outright. Uriel's own portfolio is astronomical. He guides the heavenly luminaries (1 Enoch 72:1; 79:6; 82:7) and explains why the stars' actual courses drift from the ideal Enochic calendar, tying the drift to human sin. He also shows Enoch the place prepared for the punishment of the fallen stars and Watchers (1 Enoch 18:14-19:2; 21:5-6,9), and in the Life of Adam and Eve he buries Adam together with Michael.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 9:1; 20:1-8; 40:9; 72-82 (Uriel as astronomical revealer); 4 Ezra (2 Esdras) 4:1; 10:28, where Uriel is Ezra's revealing angel throughout.

entries.title: Baal
entries.summary: The storm god of Canaan, Israel's most persistent religious rival, and Elijah's opponent on Mount Carmel.
entries.note: The storm god, and Israel's most persistent rival. The Carmel contest isn't a dispute over whether Baal exists. It is a contest over which god answers by fire, staged on a mountain and in the weather, Baal's home ground. Jehu's purge (2 Kings 10:18-28) and Josiah's reforms after it show the cult never died out between Elijah and the exile, and Elijah's "seven thousand who have not bowed" (1 Kings 19:18) is an admission of how badly Yahweh's loyalists were outnumbered.
entries.ane: The Baal Cycle from Ras Shamra has Baal defeat Yam and then Mot, build a palace, and hold kingship, the same portfolio Israel's prophets keep taking away from him. After Yam falls, Baal gets El's permission for a palace (Anat pressures El, and Asherah consents too), and Kothar-wa-Hasis builds it on the heights of Sapanu; Kothar is the same craftsman god who forged the clubs Baal used on Yam. Carmel (1 Kings 18) hits that portfolio directly. Baal is lord of fire, pictured with lightning in his hand, and Elijah calls for fire because fire is Baal's own ground. DDD traces the name back to a proper divine name in the Abu Salabikh god list of the third millennium BC, older than any Ugaritic text. Ugaritic epithets call him *bn dgn*, "son of Dagan," even though he is also counted among El's sons, and he is repeatedly titled *b'l spn*, "Baal of Zaphon," after the mountain where his palace stood. Whether Baal and Hadad were originally one god, or whether Baal was a Canaanite deity distinct from the Syrian storm god, is argued both ways; by the Iron Age the two names had split by region, Hadad for the Arameans and Baal for the Phoenicians and Canaanites.
entries.dissent: DDD's Baal article (W. Herrmann) handles the two charges against the cult differently. On child sacrifice (Jeremiah 19:5; 32:35) it is blunt: the two texts are late and evidently biased in their polemic, and without confirmation from an unsuspected source their information "should be dismissed." On cultic prostitution (Jeremiah 2:23; Hosea 2:15) it is more measured, saying the idea "should not be taken for a fact," an unproven assumption resting on two texts that are both ambiguous. Both verdicts concern the Palestinian Baal cult as history. Neither disputes that this is how Israel's prophets described it.
sources: Curtis, "Canaanite Gods and Religion," DOT:Historical Books, 136
Parker, *Ugaritic Narrative Poetry*, note-to-build: currently `kind: person`, uncurated, with a study-bible dictNote

entries.title: Baal-zebub / Beelzebul
entries.summary: A Philistine god whose name Israel deliberately misspelled into lord of the flies.
entries.note: The Hebrew form at Ekron reads "lord of flies," almost certainly a deliberate insult replacing *zebul*, "prince" or "exalted dwelling." The Greek New Testament keeps the dignified form, so the mockery belongs to Kings and not to the Gospels.
entries.invented: Treating "lord of the flies" as the god's actual name, instead of Israel's joke about him, runs the pun backward. The scholarly emendation takes "Baal-zebub" back to "Baal-zebul," "Baal the prince," with the insult made by changing one consonant. DDD traces the title behind it to the Ugaritic *zbl b'l ars*, "Prince, Lord of the Underworld," an epithet of Baal in his chthonic role as a healer invoked against disease demons. On that reading Baal-zebul was a working title for Baal the healer at Ekron, and the New Testament's *Beelzeboul* preserves the real form that Kings bent into an insult.

entries.title: Baal-peor
entries.summary: The local version of Baal tied to an incident where Israel ate meals offered to the dead.
entries.note: The local Baal of Peor, tied to the incident at Shittim. Psalm 106:28 says Israel ate sacrifices offered to the dead, which connects this cult to the Rephaim material more than to ordinary idolatry. The name Peor comes from a root meaning "open wide," used of the mouth of the netherworld in Isaiah 5:14, and it fits the Ugaritic picture of Baal going down into Mot's gullet (KTU 1.5 v:4) as well as the funerary character of the neighboring Transjordanian place names, Obot ("spirits of the dead") and Abarim ("those who have crossed over").
sources: Spronk, *Beatific Afterlife in Ancient Israel and in the Ancient Near East*

entries.title: Baal-berith
entries.summary: Lord of the covenant, worshipped at Shechem, whose temple funded a coup.
entries.note: Lord of the covenant, worshipped at Shechem, the same city where Joshua staged a covenant ceremony. Abimelech's coup is paid for out of this temple's treasury (Judges 9:4). Judges 9:46 names a second temple in the city, of "El-berith," and DDD treats it as most likely the same god under a variant title, since the narrative never distinguishes the two, though some archaeologists have argued for two shrines, one of them possibly the altar structure excavated on Mount Ebal. Israel's covenant tradition at Sinai isn't thought to be modeled on the Shechem cult; the resemblance is one of function, not descent.

entries.title: Hadad / Rimmon
entries.summary: The Syrian storm god, named when a foreign general asks to be excused for bowing in his temple.
entries.strong: H7417 (רִמּוֹן), 16 occ, mostly the place name, refs (the god): 2 Kings 5:18; Zechariah 12:11
entries.note: The Aramean storm god, Baal's Syrian counterpart, named when Naaman asks to be excused for bowing in his master's temple. Zechariah's Hadad-rimmon keeps the double name.
entries.ane: Hadad is the proper name behind the title Baal across the Levant, one storm god going by local names under the "Baal" title: Hadad in Syria, Melqart in Tyre, and on one scholarly line Chemosh in Moab and Milkom in Ammon. This file's own Chemosh and Milcom entries treat those two as separate gods and not as local Baal titles, and the tension between the sources stays on the page. DDD's Hadad article derives the name from a word for "thunderer" and follows him from Old Akkadian Adad through Ebla, Mari, and Ugarit, where he is called son of Dagan and fights Yam for a palace on Mount Sapanu in the same myth told of Baal, into the first-millennium Aramean pantheon, where he heads the pantheon at Damascus and is credited by name in the Tel Dan and Zakkur inscriptions with making and unmaking kings. DDD proposes a subsidiary deity, Hadad-milki, attested as a name element at Gozan, as the god behind the Adrammelech of 2 Kings 17:31.

entries.title: Asherah
entries.summary: A goddess and also the wooden object that stood for her, one of which sat in the Jerusalem temple.
entries.note: Both a goddess and the wooden object that stood for her, so English versions wander between "Asherah," "groves," and "poles." A carved image of her stood in the Jerusalem temple under Manasseh.
entries.ane: Athirat at Ugarit is El's consort and mother of the gods, "Lady Athirat of the Sea" and "creator of the gods," and her seventy sons make up the divine assembly; her intercession with El wins Baal his palace after Yam's defeat. The Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions naming Yahweh and "his asherah" are the most argued-over epigraphic find in this area. DDD's Asherah article adds that the Khirbet el-Qom inscription pairs the same formula with an engraved hand, an apotropaic symbol, and that both sites invoke the deity or object for blessing and protection, not polemic, so the language belonged to ordinary worshippers as well as to the Deuteronomists' opponents. Excavations at Philistine Ekron (Tel Miqne) have turned up jar inscriptions dedicated to a goddess *'srh*, which suggests her cult reached beyond Israel and Judah. Heiser reads Athirat's seventy sons against the seventy nations disinherited at Babel and allotted to the sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8-9, a deliberate rival claim in which Yahweh's council outnumbers and outranks Asherah's.
entries.dissent: Whether the inscriptions name a consort or a cult object is the argument itself, and it isn't settled. Reading *asherah* there as a proper divine name is grammatically unlikely, since Hebrew proper names don't take possessive suffixes, and that pushes most scholars toward either a cult object or a hypostatized asherah that could act as Yahweh's consort without being a fully independent goddess. DDD goes further and argues that the article/no-article distinction some scholars use to separate the goddess from the object in the Hebrew text isn't a reliable rule, since "Baal" and "Ashtoreth" both take the article as proper names elsewhere; on that reading many of the 40 occurrences stay ambiguous between goddess and object and can't be sorted cleanly.
sources: Walls, "The Gods of Israel in Comparative ANE Context," 266-267
Walton, *Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary: 1 & 2 Kings...*, 161
Heiser, *The Unseen Realm*, note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Ashtoreth / Astarte
entries.summary: A goddess of war and love whose Hebrew name was deliberately mispronounced to mean shame.
entries.note: The vowels in the Hebrew are borrowed from *boshet*, "shame," so the Masoretic pointing is itself a piece of polemic. Saul's armor is hung in her temple. DDD treats "Ashtoreth" and "Ashtaroth" as the same singular name, read as a plural only later by analogy with the generic word for "goddesses," and the usual vocalization split between the two forms is a dialect difference, not evidence of two deities.
entries.ane: Astarte is a war and love goddess across the Levant, distinct from Asherah though popular writing constantly merges them. She is the West Semitic counterpart to Ishtar and Inanna, invoked in curses to "smash an enemy's skull," pictured in Egypt as a warrior on horseback, and patron goddess of both Tyre and Sidon, Baal's consort in each, with kings styled as her priests. Her name is probably the feminine of a masculine Athtar tied to the planet Venus, so that if the morning star is the male god (compare Isaiah 14:12's "Day Star, son of Dawn") the evening star is the goddess, the same morning and evening split later attested in Greek tradition. Egyptian reliefs of Ramesses III credit her, alongside Anat, as his protective shield in battle, "Mistress of Horses, Lady of the Chariot." DDD also judges that the unnamed Queen of Heaven of Jeremiah 7 and 44 is probably Astarte and not Anat or Asherah.
sources: T. C. Mitchell, "Ashtaroth, Ashtoreth," New Bible Dictionary, 93
Joel Burnett, "Ashtoreth," Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible, 114-115

entries.title: The Queen of Heaven
entries.summary: A goddess whose cakes the women of Judah baked, and who told the prophet life was better when they did.
entries.note: Whole families bake cakes for her, and the women of Judah tell Jeremiah to his face that things went better when they did. The Masoretic vowels on her title are polemic too, like Molech's and Ashtoreth's. Read one way the title says "the Queen of Heaven"; read the way the Masoretes pointed it, it says "the work (that is, host) of heaven," turning the goddess into an abstraction. The LXX's "queen of heaven" confirms the original sense was suppressed on purpose.
entries.ane: Usually identified with Ishtar or Astarte, and the title fits both, so it reads best as a blend of the two. Ishtar's cult used cakes called *kamanu*, cognate with the Hebrew *kawwanim*, "cakes," in Jeremiah's account. Anat and Asherah also carry the title or near equivalents elsewhere in the ancient Near East, so DDD treats the identity question as secondary: by the sixth century BC "Queen of Heaven" worked as a general label for the universal mother goddess, worshipped under whatever local name suited the worshipper. A temple to the Queen of Heaven at Syene in Egypt, attested independently of Jeremiah in the fifth-century BC Hermopolis letters, sat in the same Jewish community in Egypt that Jeremiah addresses.
sources: Susan Ackerman, "Queen of Heaven," Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible, 1104

entries.title: Anat
entries.summary: A violent warrior goddess, prominent among Israel's neighbors and never once named in the Bible.
entries.note: Never named as a goddess in the Hebrew Bible, but she survives in place names and a personal name, and she is missing from the prophetic polemic despite how prominent she is at Ugarit. DDD reviews the proposed hidden references to her (Exodus 32:18, Hosea 14:9, Job 31:1, and the Beth Shan armor temple of 1 Samuel 31:10) and finds none convincing, since the Masoretic Text makes good sense without her in every case.
entries.ane: The violent warrior goddess of the Baal Cycle, who recovers Baal's body and destroys Mot. She uses bow and sword against human and divine enemies alike, backs Baal's campaign for a palace and kingship, and threatens El himself, a destroyer carrying traits usually assigned to male gods. DDD says the popular picture of Anat as Baal's sexual partner and the mother of his offspring rests on mistranslation and reconstructed gaps more than on clear text. The heifer Baal mates with in KTU 1.5 is explicitly not Anat, who searches for the pair afterward, and recent epigraphic work has removed the one tablet (KTU 1.96) once used to argue she was pregnant. She is better described as a perpetually adolescent huntress who refuses marriage and childbearing in order to stay in the male domains of war and the hunt, and in the epic of Aqhat she kills the hero for refusing to give her his bow.
sources: Peggy L. Day, "Anat," Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible, 59

entries.title: Chemosh
entries.summary: The god of Moab, and the one foreign god the Bible admits won a battle.
entries.note: The god of Moab. Jephthah argues with the Ammonites from territorial allotment, you keep what Chemosh gives you and we keep what Yahweh gives us, which is the Deuteronomy 32 worldview spoken aloud by a judge. In 2 Kings 3:27, when Mesha sacrifices his own son on the city wall in the middle of a siege, "great wrath" falls on Israel and the coalition withdraws. Nowhere else in the Old Testament is a foreign god's power against Israel conceded without qualification instead of mocked.
entries.ane: On the Mesha Stele the Moabite king credits Chemosh in language built the same way as Israel's language about Yahweh, including a *herem*. Mesha puts Nebo's people under the ban with the same root (*khrm*) as Joshua 6, blames his setbacks on Chemosh's anger the way Israel reads its fortunes through Yahweh's, and executes the population "as a spectacle for Chemosh and for Moab." No single Old Testament *herem* matches Mesha's circumstances, but the word and the practice are the same, and both sides practice functional monolatry. DDD also notes a double name on the stele, Ashtar-Chemosh (*'str.kmš*), pairing Chemosh with Ashtar, who appears in the Ugaritic Baal Cycle as a deposed and faintly ridiculous figure (KTU 1.6 i) but seems to have kept real standing on Moab's religious margins; DDD reads the pairing as strengthening Chemosh's credentials as a war god.
sources: Satterthwaite & McConville, *Exploring the Old Testament: The Histories*, 159

entries.title: Molech
entries.summary: The god associated with child sacrifice in a valley outside Jerusalem that gave us the word Gehenna.
entries.note: The vowels again come from *boshet*, and the consonants are the word for king. The cult sits in the Valley of Hinnom, where the name Gehenna comes from; Ahaz and Manasseh both burned their own sons there (2 Chronicles 28:3; 33:6), and the burning sites came to be called Topheth (Jeremiah 7:32; 19:6). Heiser ties the geography to Ugarit. Two Ugaritic snake charms locate Molech's cult at the city of Ashtaroth, and another Ugaritic text puts the god Rapiu, patron of the Rephaim, at the same city. That is the Ashtaroth linked to the Valley of the Rephaim, which Joshua 15:8 and 18:16 place right beside the Valley of Hinnom, just south of Mount Zion, Yahweh's own dwelling. On this reading Molech's Jerusalem cult was a netherworld cult with geographic and mythological logic behind its location, staged in the valley that bordered the place tied to the ancestral dead.
entries.dissent: Whether *molek* names a god or a kind of offering is a live argument, with real epigraphic evidence on the offering side. Carthaginian and Phoenician inscriptions (400-150 BC) use *mlk* as a general term for "sacrifice," but the biblical idiom "whoring after Molech" pairs that construction only with deities, images, and beings elsewhere, never with sacrifices, which argues for a real god. One resolution has an older ancient Near Eastern netherworld or ancestor-cult deity named Molek behind a later, distinctly Punic child-sacrifice rite that came to carry his name.
sources: Brian B. Schmidt, "Molech," Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible, 912
Paul E. Robertson, "Molech," Holman Illustrated Bible Dictionary, 1148
Heiser, *The Unseen Realm*, citing G. C. Heider, "Molech," DDD 2nd ed., 581-584, note-to-build: currently `kind: person`

entries.title: Milcom
entries.summary: The god of Ammon, a different god from Molech though English Bibles have blurred them.
entries.note: The god of Ammon, distinct from Molech in the Hebrew, though English versions have blurred them for centuries. Solomon builds for both in the same passage. The distinctness is itself argued. One line of evidence (2 Kings 23:10 against 23:13, where Topheth and Molech and the Mount of Olives high place and Milcom are different sites with different rites) points to two gods, while another treats Melech and Milcom as originally one Ammonite god's name, used differently at different sanctuaries, with translation flattening whatever distinction survived. DDD comes down on the two-gods side: it says there is no proof, biblical or from the Ammonite inscriptions, that Milcom is another form of Molek, and it notes that child sacrifice is never offered to Milcom anywhere in the text, only to Molech.
sources: William Henry Bennett, "Molech, Moloch," *A Dictionary of the Bible* (Hastings), 3:415
