entries.title: Dagon
entries.summary: The god of the Philistines, whose statue falls and breaks in front of Israel's ark.
entries.note: The god of the Philistines, whose statue falls twice before the ark and loses its head and hands on the threshold. The narrative is a legal scene, the vassal prostrate before his suzerain, and slapstick is the wrong reading. Dagan (Dagon is the Philistine and Hebrew form) is one of the oldest attested Semitic gods, named in third-millennium texts from Ebla and Mari a thousand years before the Philistines existed as a people, so the Philistines adopted a god already ancient in the region they settled instead of bringing him from their Aegean background.
entries.ane: At Ugarit, Dagan is a minor presence in the myths and a major one in the cult. He is called father of Baal (*bn dgn*) even though Baal is also called El's son, a tension the sources never resolve, and one of Ugarit's two main temples was his, the other being Baal's. Ugaritic texts twice call him "Dagan of Tuttul," preserving his older cult center on the Euphrates.
entries.invented: The fish-god etymology comes from Jerome and medieval commentators reading *dag*, "fish." DDD is more cautious than the earlier draft's claim that grain is more probable: it treats the fish and grain etymologies alike as unproven, since neither has solid support in the Hebrew Bible or in Mesopotamian and West Semitic sources, and it recommends resting on what is actually known, a major Amorite deity of the Mari region, instead of any etymology.

entries.title: Nisroch
entries.summary: The god in whose temple an Assyrian king was murdered by his own sons.
entries.note: Sennacherib is murdered by his sons while worshipping in this god's temple. The name doesn't appear in Assyrian sources under that spelling, which has produced a long list of proposed emendations. DDD works through and rejects Enlil, Nusku, Marduk, and a supposed Assur-Marduk blend, and lands "with reasonable certitude" on Ninurta, reading Nisroch as a scribal corruption of that god's consonants. A Neo-Assyrian letter to an unnamed king, possibly a veiled warning before the murder, independently names the assassin as Arda-Mulissi, the man the Bible calls Adrammelech, and DDD stresses that the murderer shares a name with the unrelated god Adrammelech of 2 Kings 17:31 only by coincidence.

entries.title: Nergal
entries.summary: A Mesopotamian god of plague and the underworld, brought into Samaria by resettled foreigners.
entries.note: Brought to Samaria by the men of Cuth after the deportations. In Mesopotamia he is the underworld and plague god, associated with pestilence, drought, famine, fire, and sudden death, and invoked by Assyrian and Babylonian kings on their foreign campaigns. DDD notes a chronological problem with the deportation: Cutha is absent from Sargon II's inscriptions, so its conquest and resettlement more likely belongs to Sennacherib's campaign of 703 BC, later than the Samaria deportations 2 Kings 17 otherwise describes, and the verse compresses more than one historical episode into a single sentence.
entries.ane: Ancient scribes themselves explain Nergal as "Lord of the Netherworld." He carries the epithet Meslamtaea, "the one who comes out of Emeslam," his temple at Cutha, and a Babylonian myth, Nergal and Ereshkigal, tells how he became consort of the underworld's queen. Late syncretistic texts fold him into Marduk's theology as "Marduk of battle."
sources: Mark Anthony Phelps, "Nergal," Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible, 959

entries.title: Nebo
entries.summary: The Babylonian god of scribes, shown being hauled out of town on pack animals in Isaiah's parody.
entries.strong: H5015, 13 occ, mostly the mountain and the town, refs (the god): Isaiah 46:1
entries.note: Nabu, the Babylonian god of scribes and son of Marduk, who appears as a deity exactly once, carted off on pack animals with Bel in Isaiah's parody of a divine procession. The images of Bel and Nebo were paraded through Babylon at the New Year festival, and Isaiah turns the spectacle over: the gods bow and stoop, too heavy for worn-out animals that stagger into captivity. Hauling a defeated nation's gods out of its city was a stock Mesopotamian way of mocking that nation's helplessness, and Isaiah uses it against Babylon, since a god that has to be carried can't carry anyone.
entries.ane: As scribe of the gods, Nabu wrote the tablet of destinies that recorded the fate of every person, which DDD compares to the divine record books of Exodus 32:32-33 and Psalm 69:28 and later to the book of life in Revelation 3:5 and 20:12,15. The god who kept the record of who lives and who dies goes out of the city as cargo.
sources: DDD s.v. "Nabû," 607-609, note-to-build: the entities record is `kind: place`
the deity sense needs its own record

entries.title: Bel / Marduk
entries.summary: The chief god of Babylon, named in the prophets as a god about to be humiliated.
entries.note: Bel is a title, "lord," that attaches to Marduk. Jeremiah 50:2 names both in one line, and a reader can see there that biblical polemic knows the pantheon by name. DDD notes that the public humiliation of Bel and Marduk also stands behind two works outside the Hebrew canon, the Letter of Jeremiah (Baruch 6) and the addition to Daniel called Bel and the Dragon, both long satirical demolitions of the same god.
entries.ane: Enuma Elish narrates Marduk's rise. He nets Tiamat, drives a wind into her open mouth, shoots an arrow through her swollen belly to split her heart, then slices the corpse lengthwise, using half for the roof of the sky and penning her waters so they can't escape, building order out of the chaos goddess's own body. The Babylonian Akitu festival re-enacted the myth each spring, with the king ritually humbled before Marduk's statue and the gods gathered into the city in procession, the civic pageant Isaiah 46:1-2 mocks by reducing the gods to baggage.
sources: John D. Currid, *Ancient Egypt and the Old Testament*, 39
Dalley, *Myths from Mesopotamia*, note-to-build: both currently `kind: person`

entries.title: Tammuz
entries.summary: A dying shepherd god whose women mourners Ezekiel sees weeping at the temple gate.
entries.note: Women weeping for him at the north gate of the temple, one of the four escalating abominations Ezekiel is shown. In Sumerian he is Dumuzi, "the good son" or "the right son." DDD corrects the usual description. Dumuzi wasn't originally a vegetation god; he was a shepherd god, and the vegetation traits popular writing hangs on "Tammuz" arrived later, when he absorbed Damu, a separate vegetation deity. DDD reads the next scene in the chapter, men worshipping the sun at the temple entrance (Ezekiel 8:16), as part of the same indictment of Babylonian influence spreading through Jerusalem's cult.
entries.invented: The claim that Easter descends from Tammuz worship runs through Hislop's *The Two Babylons*, which is unreliable in all its particulars. In Babylonian myth Tammuz is a beautiful shepherd killed by a boar, a winter figure whom Ishtar mourns and follows into the underworld to bring back, and Ezekiel counts the women weeping for him among the worst of the abominations. The nineteenth- and twentieth-century habit, going back to Frazer, of treating Tammuz, Osiris, Adonis, and Attis as regional versions of one universal Dying and Rising God is flagged by DDD as a category error that lumped distinct deities under one modern label.

entries.title: Adrammelech and Anammelech
entries.summary: Two gods of resettled foreigners, named in the one verse that says their people burned children to them.
entries.note: The gods of Sepharvaim, named in the one verse that says the settlers burned their children to them. Both names end in the element for "king," as Molech does. DDD reconstructs Adrammelech from West Semitic as *addir-melek*, "the glorious one is king," a royal divine title attested for Baal himself in a sixth-century BC inscription from Byblos, and not as a corruption of Hadad. Where Sepharvaim was is unresolved between a Syrian and a Babylonian candidate. This deity has nothing to do with the Adrammelech who murders Sennacherib in 2 Kings 19:37, a coincidence of names DDD flags explicitly.
sources: DDD s.v. "Adrammelech," 10, note-to-build: both currently `kind: person`

entries.title: Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Succoth-benoth
entries.summary: Four imported gods named once each and never mentioned again.
entries.strong: H807, H5026, H8662, 1 occ each; H5524, 2 occ in 1 verse
entries.note: The imported gods of the resettled north, each named once and never again. They stay as records because they are the dead ends, though DDD has more to say about each than "nothing is known." Ashima has a thin extra-biblical trail: a dedicatory inscription from the Arabian oasis of Teima invokes a god *'sym'* alongside two others, and the name may turn up again at Elephantine in the compound Eshem-Bethel. DDD floats a possible pun in Amos 8:14, where "the guilt (*'asmat*) of Samaria" may play on Ashima's name, a reading others dispute. Nibhaz is tentatively traced to an Elamite god "Ibnahaza," equated with the Babylonian water and wisdom god Ea in a cuneiform god list, the best explanation available even though nothing else is known about that god either, and the LXX's garbled "eblazer" shows the translators had no idea who he was. Tartak has two identifications on the table, both weak by DDD's own account: an Elamite deity from the same god list, or a distorted form of the Syrian goddess Atargatis. DDD calls the theory tying Tartak to Amos 8:14's "way of Beersheba" groundless. Succoth-benoth is the best attested of the four. DDD reconstructs it as Akkadian *Banitu*, "the Creatress," an epithet of Ishtar or of Marduk's consort Zarpanitu whose cult is attested as far away as the Jewish community at Syene, and it reads "Succoth" as a common noun for "image" or "stela," so the phrase means "the image of Banitu."
sources: DDD s.v. "Sukkoth-Benoth," 821, note-to-build: all four currently `kind: person` (the last stored as "Succothbenoth")

entries.title: Sikkuth and Kiyyun / Rephan
entries.summary: Star gods carried in procession, where the Greek Bible and the Hebrew give different names.
entries.strong: H5522, H3594, 1 occ each; G4481, 1 occ
entries.note: Astral deities carried in procession. Stephen quotes the Septuagint's Rephan where the Hebrew has Kiyyun, a clean, short case of the Greek Old Testament standing behind a New Testament quotation. Kiyyun is convincingly a form of Kajjamanu, the Babylonian name for Saturn ("the Steady One"), also behind the Syriac Keywan, and the LXX's Greek already shows a scribe confusing Hebrew *k* for *r*, which is how Kiyyun became Rephan, or Rompha, by the time Stephen quotes it. Sakkuth is more obscure. DDD's best match is the little-known Babylonian god Sakkud, "cupbearer of the gods," tied to the city of Der on the Elamite border, though the ancient versions (the LXX, and the Damascus Document from Qumran) read the word as "tent" or "tabernacle," "the tent of your king," and not as a divine name at all.

entries.title: Gad and Meni
entries.summary: Fortune and Destiny, two gods most readers never notice are in the verse.
entries.strong: H1409, H4507, 1 occ each as deities
entries.note: Fortune and Destiny, with a table spread and mixed wine poured for them. The Vulgate keeps only Gad as a proper name and translates Meni away. The LXX renders Gad as *daimonion* and Meni as *Tyche*, so its translators read both as real deities.
entries.ane: Gad is well attested outside Israel as a minor deity of fortune, equated with the Greek Tyche and the Latin Fortuna. Punic inscriptions from Sardinia and Ibiza pair Gad with the goddess Tanit, and Palmyrene inscriptions use "Gad" as the title of a city's own guardian spirit. Meni's Arabian counterpart is better attested still: the goddess Manat, one of the three "daughters of Allah" named in the Qur'an (53:19-20) with al-Lat and al-Uzza, appears as "Manutu" in Nabatean curse inscriptions of the first centuries BC and AD, and medieval Jewish commentators already tied Meni's name to the verb "to count, to apportion," that is, to assign a fate.

entries.title: Zeus
entries.summary: The chief Greek god, whom a crowd mistakes Barnabas for.
entries.note: The priest of Zeus brings oxen and garlands to the gates because the crowd at Lystra has decided Barnabas is Zeus and Paul is Hermes. It is one of the few places where the New Testament shows pagan devotion happening instead of describing it. Ovid's story of Philemon and Baucis, Phrygian peasants visited by Zeus and Hermes disguised as men, is a direct parallel, and DDD says the myth was well known in this region of Asia Minor and likely shaped how the Lystrans read what they saw. The rededication of the Jerusalem temple to Zeus Olympios under Antiochus IV in 168 BC (2 Maccabees 6:2) is the same event 1 Maccabees 1:54 calls, without naming Zeus, the abomination of desolation set up on the altar.
entries.ane: Hellenized Diaspora Jews sometimes called their God *Hypsistos*, "Most High," a title that had been a cultic epithet of Zeus for centuries, and the magical papyri go further and equate "Iao" (Yahweh) with Zeus directly. DDD reads both the Lystra scene and the temple rededication against this easy *interpretatio Graeca* between Zeus and Semitic sky and storm gods, Baal Shamem among them, which is why the pagan identification of Paul and Barnabas and Antiochus's rededication both felt like natural moves to outsiders, even though each drew the reaction you'd expect from the people on the receiving end.
sources: DDD s.v. "Zeus," 934-939, note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Hermes
entries.summary: The Greek messenger god, whom the same crowd mistakes Paul for because he did the talking.
entries.strong: G2060, 2 occ (one is a human name in Romans 16:14)
entries.note: Paul is taken for Hermes because he was doing the talking, the detail Luke bothers to include. DDD shows how exact the fit is. Plato already defined Hermes as *hermeneus*, "interpreter," and *angelos*, "messenger," because his whole mythic portfolio, inventor of the lyre, patron of oratory and persuasion, guide and go-between, turns on eloquence, the quality Acts 14:12 picks out in Paul ("because he was the chief speaker").

entries.title: Artemis of the Ephesians
entries.summary: A local goddess whose souvenir trade started a riot against Paul.
entries.note: The riot is economic before it is theological, since Demetrius's silversmiths are losing a trade. The city clerk calms the crowd by appealing to the image that fell from heaven, using *diopetes*, "fallen from Zeus" (Acts 19:35), a stock claim for statues believed to be made by the gods and not by human hands, which was the very point Paul had been attacking. DDD notes that about twenty-five other gods were worshipped in Ephesus at the time. The riot wasn't provoked by monotheism threatening polytheism in general, then, but by Paul's claim that a handmade object can't be a god.
entries.ane: The Ephesian Artemis is a local cult figure and not the huntress of classical Greek myth. She absorbed an older Anatolian mother and fertility goddess, possibly named Upis, and her temple, one of the Seven Wonders, doubled as the city's bank and a place of asylum, so the silversmiths' riot was also a defense of Ephesus's financial center. Her cult title *Megale*, "Great," behind the crowd's "great is Artemis of the Ephesians" (Acts 19:27-28), set her above every other Ephesian deity in rank without making her the only one.
sources: DDD s.v. "Artemis," 91-96, note-to-build: entities.json has `Diana` (the Vulgate and KJV name) as `kind: person` but not Artemis

entries.title: The Dioscuri
entries.summary: Twin gods who protected sailors, carved on the ship that carried Paul to Rome.
entries.note: Castor and Pollux, the figurehead on the ship that carries Paul from Malta, patron gods of sailors, and Luke records the detail without comment. DDD explains why sailors trusted them in particular. The twins were credited with appearing as St. Elmo's fire, the electrical glow sailors saw at a masthead in a storm, taken as a sign the Dioscuri had come to save the crew, so they were carved on a ship's prow. Their name, "youths of Zeus," also survives as a month name in the dating formula of 2 Maccabees 11:21.

entries.title: The unknown god
entries.summary: An Athenian altar hedging against offending a god nobody could name, which Paul preached from.
entries.note: Paul takes an Athenian hedge against offending an unnamed deity and preaches from it, and his quotation of Aratus two verses later makes the same move in the other direction. DDD confirms the practice was real and not a Lukan invention. The second-century traveler Pausanias independently records altars "to unknown gods" near the harbor at Phalerum and beside the great altar of Zeus at Olympia, and an older tradition preserved by Diogenes Laertius traces the custom to the sixth century BC, when the seer Epimenides of Cnossos ended a plague in Athens by releasing sheep and building unmarked altars wherever each one lay down, so as not to offend a god whose name the city didn't know.

entries.title: The python spirit
entries.summary: A fortune-telling spirit named after the oracle at Delphi, cast out of a slave girl.
entries.note: The Greek says a spirit, a python, the term for the Delphic oracle. Luke doesn't call the girl a fraud; he has Paul cast out the thing that made her accurate. DDD traces how the word got there. Python was the dragon Apollo killed to take over the sanctuary at Delphi, and the name drifted through the oracular priestess who spoke there, the Pythia, into a general label for any prophesying spirit or medium by the first century AD. The Vulgate uses the same word to translate the "medium or necromancer" of Leviticus 20:27 (*pythonicus spiritus*), which shows the term had become fully generic and gives this entry a second biblical anchor beyond Acts.

entries.title: Mot
entries.summary: Death as a figure with an open throat that is never full.
entries.note: Death with an open throat that is never full, a covenant made with Death, Death climbing in through the windows. The argument is over whether these are personification or a live memory of the god.
entries.ane: Mot is Baal's last adversary at Ugarit and swallows him. His voracious appetite matches the biblical language about Sheol closely enough that mythological influence is plausible, though disputed, and Mot likely received no cult in Israel or Judah. DDD's entry on the "firstborn of Death" of Job 18:13 confirms this from the Ugaritic side: Mot carries the epithets "son of El" and "Beloved of El," yet he is absent from every Ugaritic pantheon list, sacrificial list, and offering list, and no sanctuary of his has turned up at Ugarit. Job 18:13's *bekor mawet* draws on the same figure, and DDD lays out three readings. The phrase may be an idiom for a deadly disease; it may name an actual offspring demon of Mot, on the model of the Mesopotamian Namtar, Ereshkigal's vizier; or it may be an attributive genitive, "Firstborn Death," a title for Mot himself as El's firstborn, which N. Wyatt argues from "Beloved of El" being a legitimation formula and not a term of affection. Isaiah 28:15's covenant with Death is almost universally read as something other than the Ugaritic god, either a foreign nation or a pun on the Egyptian goddess Mut, guarantor of treaties, and since it goes beyond simple personification without clear Ugaritic precedent for a death-covenant, it may be a Hebrew innovation instead of borrowed myth.
sources: T. J. Lewis, "First-Born of Death," DDD, 332-334

entries.title: Yam
entries.summary: The sea as an opponent God fights, not just water.
entries.strong: H3220 (יָם), 396 occ, nearly all the ordinary sea, refs (the power): Job 7:12; Job 26:12; Psalm 74:13; Psalm 89:9-10; Habakkuk 3:8; 1 Kings 7:23-26
entries.note: God rebukes the sea, splits the sea, tramples the waves, and the Hebrew poetry keeps leaving open whether the sea is scenery or an opponent.
entries.ane: Yam is Baal's first rival in the Ugaritic cycle. He falls to two named weapons that Kothar forges and speaks incantations over: Yagrush, "Driver," which fails to fell him, and then Ayyamarri, which strikes him between the eyes and drops him (KTU 1.2 IV). His Ugaritic title is *zbl ym tpt nhr*, "Prince Sea, Judge River," so the sea and the river flood are one power under two names. An eighteenth-century BC letter from Mari, quoting Nur-Sin of Aleppo to King Zimri-Lim, has the storm god say "the weapons with which I had battled against Sea I gave to you," the earliest literary witness to the Baal and Yam combat, centuries older than the Ugaritic tablets. In Israel's cultic poetry the sea is a personified combatant alongside Tannin, Leviathan, and Rahab: Yahweh rebukes it, smashes its heads, dries up its waters or sets their limits. Psalm 74 pictures a battle before creation that splits the personified *yam*, matching Ugaritic Yam, and in the same breath the sea serves as backdrop and as an opponent with real agency. The temple furniture keeps the image. Solomon's molten sea (1 Kings 7:23-26; 2 Chronicles 4:2-10), a bronze basin about fifteen feet across standing on twelve bronze bulls, put the cosmic Sea, tamed and domesticated, inside Yahweh's house.
sources: F. Stolz, "Sea," DDD, 737-741 (the bronze sea and Yam's title *zbl ym tpt nhr* come later in the same long article)
Dempsey Rosales Acosta, "Lord of Hosts," *Lexham Bible Dictionary*
M. S. Smith, *The Ugaritic Baal Cycle*, Vol. I, on KTU 1.1-1.2

entries.title: Leviathan
entries.summary: A sea monster God crushes in one poem and plays with in another.
entries.strong: H3882 (לִוְיָתָן), 6 occ in 5 verses (Isaiah 27:1 names it twice)
entries.note: Six occurrences in five verses, and they don't all describe the same kind of thing. Psalm 74 has God crushing its heads, Psalm 104 has it playing in the sea God made for it, and Isaiah 27 puts its death in the future. Amos 9:3 belongs beside these without being an occurrence of the word: its serpent at the bottom of the sea is a *nachash*, not a *livyatan*, and DDD's Leviathan article cites it as a mere snake on the sea floor, the dedramatized end of the tradition, against the Psalm 74 and Isaiah 27 texts that blend history and myth to magnify the monster and so magnify Yahweh. The Septuagint still renders that snake *drakon*, the word it uses for Leviathan and the other chaos monsters, so the two sit in one semantic field even where the theology has drained out. Job 3:8 assumes a working trade in Leviathan magic, people "skilled in rousing up Leviathan," a curse technique still attested in later Jewish Aramaic incantation bowls. Psalm 104:26 goes further than taming it and makes Leviathan a creature Yahweh formed to play with; the Hebrew is ambiguous between God playing with Leviathan and Leviathan playing in the sea, and rabbinic tradition chose the first and set it in the last three hours of the day. Later tradition (1 Enoch 60:7-9,24) makes Leviathan female and Behemoth male, Leviathan in the watery abyss and Behemoth in a hidden desert to the east, both fattened as food for the righteous at the end.
entries.ane: Litan, the fleeing, twisting serpent, appears in the Baal Cycle in wording close enough to Isaiah 27:1 to set the two side by side: "when you killed Litan, the fleeing serpent, annihilated the twisty serpent, the potentate with seven heads," which maps almost word for word onto Isaiah's "fleeing" and "twisting" serpent. Both texts have a coiling serpent defeated by a storm deity establishing order, and the match runs down to the vocabulary. Psalm 74:13-14 names Yam, the plural "dragons," and Leviathan together as one chaos cluster crushed at creation and handed over as food to desert creatures, the same triad and the same turn from defeated enemy into food found at Ugarit.
entries.invented: Leviathan as a surviving dinosaur, and the fire-breathing lines of Job 41 read as zoology, a young-earth apologetic imported into a poem. The crocodile identification of Job 40:25-41:26 goes back to Samuel Bochart's *Hierozoicon* of 1663 and not to modern paleontology.
sources: J. W. van Henten, "Dragon," DDD, 265-266 (the LXX's *drakon* for the *nachash* of Amos 9:3), note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Behemoth
entries.summary: A huge land beast in Job that nobody has been able to identify.
entries.note: A plural form used as a singular, which is part of why the identification is hard. Hippopotamus, elephant, and mythic bull have all been proposed, and each one strains some part of the description.
entries.ane: Marvin Pope's proposed Ugaritic ancestor is "El's calf Atik," also called Arshu, paired in the Baal Cycle with a seven-headed sea dragon and defeated by Anat in the same boast: "I smote Ar[shu] beloved of El, I put an end to El's calf Atik" (KTU 1.3 iii:43-44), right after she claims the dragon. The pairing follows Job 40-41's own order, an ox-like land beast beside a sea monster. Egypt had a ritual answer that suits the hippopotamus reading, a festival where a hippo was killed ceremonially as a stand-in for pharaoh's enemies, on top of the animal's usual role in Egyptian myth as a hostile power against the throne. Later Jewish tradition (1 Enoch 60:7-9) makes the pair explicit and geographic, Behemoth male and in the desert east of Eden, Leviathan female and in the abyss, both fattened for the righteous at the end-time banquet (also 2 Baruch 29:4; 4 Ezra 6:49-52).
entries.invented: The sauropod reading, which needs the tail like a cedar to be a neck and ignores the rest of the passage. The hippopotamus reading has its own problem, since the text stresses Behemoth's visible genitals and a hippo's are internal and mostly underwater. Grammatically *behemoth* is the intensive feminine plural of "beast," yet every verb and pronoun for it in Job 40 is masculine singular, a plural-form name for a singular, mythic super-ox, and nowhere else in the Old Testament does the word work as a proper name. G. R. Driver's rival crocodile reading has to emend the Masoretic Text to get there, swapping which word eats which ("he eats cattle like grass" for "he eats grass like cattle").
sources: Matthews/Chavalas/Walton, *IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT*, on Job 40:15-24

entries.title: Rahab
entries.summary: A chaos monster God cuts to pieces, and also a nickname for Egypt.
entries.note: A chaos figure God cuts to pieces, and also a code name for Egypt. The two senses are connected, and Isaiah 51:9 uses the sea monster's defeat to mean the Exodus. Job 9:13 has "the helpers of Rahab" bowing beneath God, an army of lesser monsters that DDD sets beside Tiamat's monster army in Enuma Elish and the "Big Ones" who back Yam against Baal at Ugarit (KTU 1.3 iii:38ff). The plural *rehabim* appears once more, in Psalm 40:5, for the false and demonic powers a faithful Israelite doesn't turn to.
entries.invented: Rahab of Jericho is a different word with different consonants and no relation: she is *rachav* (רָחָב), the chaos monster is *rahav* (רַהַב), a *chet* against a *he*. Every use of the monster leans toward the Exodus defeat of Egypt more than toward creation's ordering of chaos, and Isaiah 51:9's monster-slaying runs straight into 51:10's crossing of the sea. The name carries "inflation" and "pride" (Egyptian "boisterousness"), and Isaiah recasts Egypt as "Rahab who sits still," a blustering power that can't deliver. DDD notes the name has no real Semitic cognate apart from a possible Akkadian variant of the chaos monster Labbu, and it prefers a derivation from Hebrew *rahav*, "assail, press," paired with Akkadian *ra'abu*, "tremble," whose derivative *rubu* covers both rage and floodwater. Rahab keeps turning up wet.
sources: M. J. Evans, "Rahab," New Dictionary of Biblical Theology, 715

entries.title: Tannin
entries.summary: Sea monsters, which Genesis pointedly lists among the things God made and called good.
entries.note: Genesis 1:21 puts the great *tannin* in the column of things created and called good, which reads as deliberate given what the word does everywhere else, and Psalm 148:7 goes a step further and calls the *tanninim* into the choir of creation praising Yahweh. Ezekiel calls Pharaoh one twice (29:3; 32:2), and in Jeremiah 51:34 Zion says Nebuchadnezzar "swallowed me like the tannin," so the same word serves for sea monster, Egypt, and Babylon depending on the enemy in view. Where Tiamat is destroyed outright in Enuma Elish, Genesis separates and bounds the elements outside order (darkness, the deep) without annihilating them, and Yahweh creates the sea monsters as what they are, not as beings gone wrong. They belong to the plan instead of standing in its way, and that departs from the rest of the ancient Near East, where such creatures sit outside the divine order.
sources: John H. Walton and J. Harvey Walton, *Demons and Spirits in Biblical Theology*, 100-101

entries.title: Resheph
entries.summary: A plague god reduced in the Bible to a word for disease, who still walks at God's feet in one poem.
entries.note: Usually translated plague, flame, or burning coal. In Habakkuk 3:5 he walks at Yahweh's feet beside Deber, which is hard to read as an abstract noun.
entries.ane: Resheph is a well-attested plague and war god across the Levant and into Egypt. An Ugaritic pantheon list identifies him with Nergal, and the Keret poem casts him as a plague god striking the king's household (KTU 1.14 i:18-19). He appears in the Amarna letters too (EA 35). Mot had no offspring at all, according to DDD's "First-Born of Death" article, but Resheph was thought to have children, the premise behind Job 5:7's "sons of Resheph" flying up like sparks. In Habakkuk 3:5 he becomes a henchman in Yahweh's retinue, possibly one of two warrior gods, with Deber, flanking Yahweh, matching the Ugaritic Resheph and Deber as gods of war and destruction. Biblical usage keeps the name subordinate throughout. It is demythologized and attached to plague and disaster without acting as an independent agent, so death and disease stay under Yahweh's sole authority, the same demotion Deber and Qeteb get below.

entries.title: Deber and Qeteb
entries.summary: Pestilence and Destruction, named in a psalm in a way that sounds like a list of beings.
entries.note: Pestilence and Destruction. Psalm 91 lists four threats in a shape that reads like a catalogue of named powers, and Habakkuk marches Deber in front of Yahweh as an attendant beside Resheph, matching the Ugaritic pairing of the two as gods of war and destruction, though the Hebrew Bible consistently strips them of independent agency. DDD's Qeteb entry reads Psalm 91:5-6 as one unit: the terror of the night, the arrow that flies by day, Deber stalking in the darkness, and Qeteb laying waste at noon. Deber is apparently Resheph's nocturnal double and the arrow his daytime weapon, so the four may reduce to two gods working night and day shifts. Qeteb turns up a fourth time at Isaiah 28:2, where "a tempest of Qeteb" drives a hailstorm against Ephraim, another case of Yahweh's judgment arriving under a demoted Canaanite destroyer's name. The Septuagint translates Qeteb differently in each of its four occurrences, a sign that its translators no longer treated the word as a fixed divine name.

entries.title: Shahar and Shalem
entries.summary: Dawn and Dusk as divine figures, one of whom is the father of the shining one in Isaiah 14.
entries.note: Dawn and Dusk. *Helel ben-shahar* in Isaiah 14:12 is the son of Shahar, and that only means something if Shahar is a figure. The Ugaritic texts make them a divine pair, fathered by Ilu (El) on two women he meets by the shore in KTU 1.23 ("The Gracious and Beautiful Gods," lines 49-54), nursed by "the Lady" (Anat or Athirat), and sharing Mot's insatiable appetite, "one lip to the earth, one lip to the heavens." With Shahar named in Isaiah 14:12, a cult of Shalem is plausible, though the direct evidence is thin. DDD's own Shahar entry reads most of dawn's other biblical appearances as poetry and not theology: in Job 38:12 dawn is God's creature taking its post and no rival; in Psalm 139:9 the "wings of the dawn" mark the world's eastern edge inside a cosmological psalm without implying a goddess; and Song of Songs 6:10, the bride "fair as the dawn," is the one place DDD grants that a goddess would fit the imagery better than a god, if any of these passages is doing double duty.
entries.ane: In the Ugaritic god list KTU 1.123:11, Shahru and Shalimu appear among the paired divine couples, and in KTU 1.107 and 1.100 they join the sun goddess in collecting, or failing to dispose of, snake venom, an odd but consistent job that gives them a role in poison alongside dawn and dusk. Mark Smith's Baal Cycle commentary notes that El's fathering of the pair in KTU 1.23:48-54 is one of the few solid signs that El's family had any astral character at all, and ties the pair to Venus as morning and evening star, the identification behind their epithet "the gracious gods" (*'ilm n'mm*, KTU 1.23:60,67).
sources: M. S. Smith, *The Ugaritic Baal Cycle*, Vol. II, on Athtar and the family of El ---

entries.title: The Watchers (Enochic)
entries.summary: Angels who, in 1 Enoch, come down to earth, marry women, and teach humanity things it should not know.
entries.note: The canonical term is neutral, Aramaic, and appears only in Daniel 4. The fallen sense comes from 1 Enoch, where two hundred of them descend on Hermon under an oath and name the mountain for the curse they bound on it (1 Enoch 6:6). Nickelsburg's translation shows the account weaves two sources together, a Shemihazah strand about marriage and monstrous offspring and an Asael strand about forbidden teaching, following Collins's analysis as Heiser quotes it at length. The offspring chain runs three generations in 1 Enoch 7:2: the Watchers father giants, the giants father Nephilim, and the Nephilim father Elioud, a term with no biblical counterpart.
entries.ane: The Mesopotamian apkallu, seven divine sages created in the primeval Abyss and sent by Ea (Enki) to civilize humanity before the Flood, are the template the Watcher story inverts. Cuneiform tradition names four post-Flood apkallu as "of human descent," the fourth only "two-thirds apkallu," the same hybrid status 1 Enoch gives the Watchers' giant sons. A ritual text from Assur (KAR 298) calls protective apkallu figurines *massare*, "watchers," the same idea as the Aramaic *'yryn*, "wakeful ones," that 1 Enoch and Daniel use, so the word "Watcher" carries the Mesopotamian guardian-sage concept into Jewish demonology as a deliberate, polemical inversion.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 6-16; Jubilees 4-5; 4QEn-a from Qumran, on which the Hermon geography depends because the Ethiopic is corrupt at 1 Enoch 6:6; 4Q530 (the Book of Giants) mentions "gardeners" tending trees, an image tied to the Watchers before their fall.
entries.dissent: How much of Enoch's expansion Jude and 2 Peter actually endorse is argued.
sources: DDD s.v. "Watcher," 893-894, note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Shemihazah
entries.summary: The leader who talks the other Watchers into the descent and binds them to an oath.
entries.note: The leader who proposes the descent and binds the others to a mutual oath so none can back out. He isn't named in the Bible. 1 Enoch 6:7-8 gives a roster of twenty chiefs of ten under him (Arteqoph, Remashel, Kokabel, and the rest), and 1 Enoch 8:3 credits him personally with teaching spells and root-cutting, separate from Asael's teaching of crafts. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan later names him as "Shamhazai" at Genesis 6, pairing him with Azael as the two fallen angels that Targum is willing to name, where Targum Onqelos avoids the fallen-angel reading altogether.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 6:3-8; 1 Enoch 8:3; 1 Enoch 10:11.
sources: Collins, quoted in Heiser, *Reversing Hermon*, ch. 2
DDD s.v. "Nephilim," 618-619 (the naming in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan)

entries.title: Asael
entries.summary: The Watcher who teaches weapons and cosmetics and gets buried under rocks until judgment.
entries.note: The Watcher who teaches metalwork, weapons, and cosmetics, and is bound hand and foot and thrown into darkness at Dudael. He is often connected to the Azazel of Leviticus 16. In 1 Enoch 10:4-6 the Lord sends Raphael to bind him, cast him into a desert pit at Dudael, and cover him with jagged rocks so he can't see light until the judgment, which is where 1 Enoch moves Azazel from a ritual term for unholy ground to the leader of evil supernatural forces. The link to Leviticus 16 is firmer than a guess. DDD's Azazel article treats 1 Enoch 8:1 (metalworking) and 9:6 (revealing heavenly secrets and enticing to injustice) as the same demonizing path, and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan at Genesis 6 names the two lead fallen angels "Shamhazai and Azael," using the consonants of Leviticus's Azazel.
sources: Hanson, "Rebellion in Heaven, Azazel and Euhemeristic Heroes in 1 Enoch 6-11," JBL 96 (1977): 195-233

entries.title: Azazel
entries.summary: The name on the second lot at the Day of Atonement, where the other lot says God.
entries.strong: H5799 (עֲזָאזֵל), 4 occ in 3 verses (Leviticus 16:10 uses the name twice)
entries.note: Every occurrence falls in the Day of Atonement ritual. The lots are cast "for Yahweh" and "for Azazel," and the parallel makes the place reading hard to hold, since the other lot is no place.
entries.secondTemple: Azazel's demonization intensifies under dualistic influence in 1 Enoch (8:1; 9:6; 10:4-8; 13:1) and the Apocalypse of Abraham, where he appears as an unclean bird, "lord of the heathens" (22:6), and as the serpent who tempts Eve in paradise (23:5,9); the Messiah judges him with his company (1 Enoch 55:4).
entries.dissent: Place name, abstract noun ("complete removal"), and personal name all have defenders, and the older English versions chose the abstraction and gave us "scapegoat." The Masoretic Text keeps *aza'zel* as a single word, and the parallel structure of the two lots is itself an argument for the personal name: Yahweh is a proper name, and Hebrew parallelism suggests its counterpart is one too. On that reading the ritual doesn't offer anything to Azazel. It sends the sin-goat into territory under his jurisdiction, outside land held holy for Yahweh. The LXX's *apopompe*, "sending away," is the likely root of "scapegoat" through *'ez* plus *'zl*, "the goat that goes away." William Tyndale coined the English word "scapegoat" in his 1530 Pentateuch, building the compound to capture the ritual's function instead of transliterating Azazel or leaving it untranslated, and Symmachus, Aquila, the Vulgate, and later Luther all read the term as the goat's action rather than a being's name. DDD sorts the scholarship into three models: a nomadic desert-demon reading (the goat is sent to Azazel in the wilderness); an Egyptian derivation (Görg's *'d3-dr*, "the expelled culprit," tied to Seth); and a background in South Anatolian and North Syrian elimination rites with Hittite and Hurrian parallels from Kizzuwatna, which DDD's contributor judges the most plausible both conceptually and philologically. On that reconstruction, the desert-demon reading isn't original to Leviticus 16 but grew up as the chapter's tradition formed, once postexilic monotheism needed to interpret an inherited ritual term.

entries.title: Nephilim
entries.summary: The giants of Genesis 6, born from the sons of God and human women.
entries.strong: H5303 (נְפִילִים), 3 occ in 2 verses (Numbers 13:33 uses the word twice)
entries.note: Two verses in the whole Hebrew Bible, with a third, disputed, at Ezekiel 32:27. Genesis 6:4 says they were on the earth in those days "and also afterward," the clause the report in Numbers 13 depends on. 1 Enoch 7:2 spells out the lineage, Watchers to giants to Nephilim to Elioud, a three-generation chain with no biblical parallel.
entries.ane: Anne Draffkorn Kilmer proposed identifying the Nephilim with the Mesopotamian apkallu, the antediluvian culture heroes who, according to Berossus, brought the arts of civilization to humankind; both traditions make the generation after the catastrophe hybrid and diminished.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 7 and Jubilees 7 both give the offspring reading, the oldest interpretation on record. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names the fallen angels of Genesis 6 as "Shamhazai and Azael," where Targum Onqelos uses *gbry'*, "mighty ones," to avoid the fallen-angel reading. 4QEnGiants 3:8 calls the offspring "the Nephilim of the earth" (*npyly 'r'*), stressing their earthbound activity despite their heavenly origin.
entries.dissent: Whether *nephilim* comes from *naphal*, "to fall," or is a loanword is unresolved. A third proposal from *pala'*, "extraordinary," has little support, and the term's precise meaning likely vanished with the pre-Israelite dialects that disappeared after the conquest. Heiser argues from spelling. The Hebrew has two forms, *nephilim* and *nephiylim* (Numbers 13:33), and the *y* in the second marks a long vowel that rules out *naphal*, which would give *nephulim*. He proposes an Aramaic loanword, *naphiyla*, "giant," picked up in the exile, which pluralizes in Hebrew to exactly the *nephiylim* spelling of Numbers 13:33 and explains why the Septuagint translators consistently rendered the word "giants."
entries.invented: Ancient-astronaut readings, and the Sethite reading that needs the word to mean nothing more than "fallen men."
refs: Ezekiel 32:27 (contested: *gibborim nophelim*, "the fallen warriors," may keep the mythic sense without naming the group)
sources: Heiser, *Reversing Hermon*, ch. 1, note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Gibborim
entries.summary: The mighty men of old, a word used of ordinary warriors too.
entries.note: The mighty men of old, the men of renown. The same word describes David's warriors, so it carries no supernatural weight by itself, and Genesis 6:4 supplies that from context. Ezekiel 32:17-32 gives the gibborim a place of honor in Sheol, lying in state with their swords under their heads and their shields over their bones, and Sirach 16:7 glosses the same tradition, saying they rebelled trusting in their strength. The first named *gibbor*, Nimrod (Genesis 10:8), carries an epithet cognate with Akkadian *gabbaru*, "strong," and Arabic *al-jabbar*, "the giant," which is also a name for the constellation Orion.

entries.title: Rephaim
entries.summary: A people of giants in some texts and the shades of the dead in others.
entries.note: A pre-Israelite population in the conquest texts and the shades of the dead in the poetry, and the overlap is no accident of translation. Isaiah 14:9 has Sheol stirring up the Rephaim to meet the arriving king. Proverbs uses the term three times as a byword for death: Lady Folly's house "sinks down to the Rephaim" (2:18), her guests are already "in the depths of Sheol" (9:18), and the man who strays "will rest in the assembly of the Rephaim" (21:16). Job 26:5 puts them "beneath the waters," under Sheol, and Psalm 88:10 asks whether the departed will ever rise up to praise God, expecting the answer no. The Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem (Joshua 15:8; 18:16; 2 Samuel 5:18) adjoins the Valley of Hinnom, where the name Gehenna comes from, so the underworld association is geographic as well as poetic.
entries.ane: The Ugaritic *rpum* are a company of the honored dead tied to the royal cult in Bashan, among other places. Og of Bashan, "a survivor of the Rephaim," lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei, which the Ugaritic tablets name as the seat of *mlk*, the deified king and eponym of the *mlkm*, the *rpum*, so "the land of the Rephaim" could as easily read "the underworld of the Rephaim." DDD's contributor argues that Baal himself carries the epithet *rpu*, "healer," as lord over the *rpum* in three fragmentary Ugaritic ritual texts: KTU 1.20-22, "the Rephaim text"; KTU 1.108, a banquet liturgy for the royal dead; and KTU 1.161, a funeral rite for a recently dead king. All three are built around invitations to the *rpum* to come up and feast, and scholars read them variously as evidence for periodic communion between the living king and his royal ancestors or as commemoration only.
entries.secondTemple: The ancient versions merge the Rephaim and the Nephilim. The LXX and Vulgate usually render *repha'im* as "giants," and rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabbah 26:7; 31:12; Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer 34) holds that Rephaim was simply another name for the Nephilim, whose monstrous offspring were cast into the netherworld according to 1 Enoch 6-14, offered as the reason they could be called "healers" at all.
sources: Heiser, *Reversing Hermon*, 91-92, ch. 6 ("Old Testament Bashan: Giants and the Underworld"), note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Anakim
entries.summary: The giant clan at Hebron whose size made the Israelite spies call themselves grasshoppers.
entries.note: The descendants of Anak at Hebron, compared to the Rephaim in Deuteronomy 2:11 and connected to the Nephilim in Numbers 13:33. Joshua 11:22 notes the survivors left in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod, and Gath is where Goliath comes from; Walton's commentary on 1 Samuel 27:2-3 confirms that Gath's existence before the Philistines is traditionally tied to the Canaanite Anakim. The conquest's *herem* language targets these bloodlines in particular. Joshua 11:21-22 names the Anakim as the object of the campaign in both the southern and northern theaters, and the note that survivors remained "only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod" sets up the Goliath story generations later. DDD classes the Anakim, builders of fortified cities in southern Judah, as Rephaim under a nickname that alludes to their size, and note that the LXX mechanically renders *nephilim*, *repha'im*, "sons of Rapha," *'anaqim*, and *gibborim* all as *gigantes*.
entries.dissent: A speculative and little-followed proposal (MacLaurin, cited in Heiser's companion notes to *The Unseen Realm*) connects *'anaqim* to *seranim*, the title of the Philistine rulers, and through it to the Aegean Sea Peoples. The overlap of Anakim and Philistines at Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod is real; the linguistic link isn't established.
sources: DDD s.v. "Rephaim," 692-699 (the Anakim are discussed under this entry, with no separate article)
Walton, *IVP Bible Background Commentary*, 1 Samuel 27:2-3, note-to-build: currently `kind: person`

entries.title: Emim, Zamzummim, Zuzim
entries.summary: What Moab and Ammon called the same giants everyone else called Rephaim.
entries.note: Regional names for one phenomenon. Moab called them Emim, Ammon called them Zamzummim, and Deuteronomy counts both as Rephaim, so the passage is a gazetteer of what different peoples called the giants. DDD's Zamzummim article derives the name from the root *ZMM*, "to plot evil," and, following Hübner, reads the Zamzummim as originally underworld spirits comparable to Og and "the Molek of Bashan," not as a folk-etymology joke about unintelligible speech. The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen 21:29) preserves a scribe's own uncertainty about the Zuzim. He first wrote the name as *ynwzny'*, then added a *mem* above the line to correct it to *zumzammaye*, in effect admitting he couldn't identify the Zuzim of Genesis 14:5 any other way and equating them with the better-known Zamzummim of Deuteronomy 2:20.
entries.ane: DDD's Zamzummim article notes that they appear in no extra-biblical text, so unlike the Rephaim (Ugaritic *rpum*) they have no comparative Near Eastern evidence beyond the etymology of the name.
sources: DDD's "Emim" entry is only a cross-reference to "Rephaim" (299)

entries.title: Og of Bashan
entries.summary: A giant king whose iron bed was thirteen feet long.
entries.note: The last of the Rephaim, whose iron bed is nine cubits long (about thirteen feet) and four wide (about six), ruling Bashan, the region the Ugaritic texts associate with the dead and the gates of the underworld. His defeat is recited in the Psalms as a founding victory. Walton's commentary flags that the bed's dimensions match Marduk's cultic bed in the Esagila temple in Babylon exactly, where Marduk and his consort Zarpanitu met once a year in a sacred marriage meant to secure the land's blessing and hold the cosmic order in place. Heiser reads the match as a deliberate polemical link back to the apkallu and Watcher material of Genesis 6, which makes Og heir to Babylon's antediluvian divine knowledge. DDD's Bashan article adds that Psalm 68:15-16 calls Bashan itself a *har elohim*, "mountain of God," language otherwise reserved for Yahweh's own dwelling, and that the region's Ugaritic place names (Ashtaroth, Edrei) mark it as the seat of the deified dead kings, the *mlkm* and *rpum*, making Bashan a Canaanite heaven and hell at once.
entries.dissent: Some commentators and translations read Deuteronomy 3:11's *'eres barzel* as a basalt sarcophagus instead of a literal iron bed. Walton's commentary judges the plain meaning clear enough and keeps "iron bed," noting that iron was still a precious, remarkable material in the period, comparable to the gold- and ivory-overlaid furniture described elsewhere.

entries.title: Goliath and the sons of Rapha
entries.summary: The giant David killed, and the relatives of his who show up later in the same books.
entries.strong: H1555 (Goliath), 6 occ; H5593 (Saph), 1 occ; H3902 (Lahmi), 1 occ
entries.note: 2 Samuel 21 lists four descendants of Rapha at Gath: Ishbi-benob, killed by Abishai (21:16-17); Saph, or Sippai, killed by Sibbecai (21:18; 1 Chronicles 20:4); a third killed by Elhanan (21:19; 1 Chronicles 20:5); and an unnamed giant with six fingers and six toes, killed by David's nephew Jonathan (21:20-21; 1 Chronicles 20:6-7). The Elhanan verse is a well-known textual crux. The Masoretic 2 Samuel 21:19 has Elhanan striking down "Goliath the Gittite" in the words used of David's kill, while 1 Chronicles 20:5 has him striking down "Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite," which most text critics take as the earlier or corrected reading, since otherwise 2 Samuel credits two different men with killing the same giant. Goliath is the last of a line the text is closing out, and Walton's commentary on 1 Samuel ties his city to the conquest-era remnant, noting that Gath's pre-Philistine existence is traditionally connected to the Canaanite Anakim (Joshua 11:22). DDD's Rapha article records de Moor's speculative proposal that a garbled Amos 5:26 once read "the star of your god Rapha," though the LXX's Raiphan or Rephan makes that unlikely.
entries.dissent: The Masoretic Text gives Goliath's height as six cubits and a span, about 9'9" at an 18-inch cubit and a 9-inch span; the Septuagint, 4QSam-a (the only Hebrew Dead Sea Scrolls witness to the verse), and Josephus all read four cubits and a span, about 6'9". The difference is two cubits, three feet, and a real textual problem. The case for the shorter reading is J. Daniel Hays's, who argues that the Masoretic number is a scribal error and that the Qumran and Greek evidence preserves the better text. Clyde Billington answered him in the same journal, arguing that the two readings don't conflict at all. The Septuagint translator worked in Alexandria, where the royal Egyptian cubit of 20.65 inches was the standard, and converted the Hebrew text's common cubits into royal ones; at four royal cubits and a span Goliath comes out a little over 7'8". Billington concludes that the Masoretic six cubits is original and that Goliath stood just over eight feet, measured in a common cubit of about sixteen inches, and Hays replied in the same issue. The Greek tradition isn't uniform either, since some Septuagint witnesses read six cubits and Codex Venetus reads five. Even at four cubits Goliath towers over his period, whose male skeletal remains run under 5'6". Ishbi-benob's spear is said to weigh three hundred shekels, about half the weight given for Goliath's in 1 Samuel 17:7, keeping the whole clan's scale consistent. A widely repeated claim about two seven-foot female skeletons found at Tell es-Sa'idiyeh traces to a misheard museum lecture and not to any publication; Heiser corresponded with the excavator at the British Museum in 2014, who confirmed no such skeletons exist. Rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah) goes further and makes Orpah, Ruth's sister-in-law, the mother of Goliath and his brothers, her Moabite ancestry carrying the blood of the Emim giants, with a pun on her having kissed (*nashaq*) Naomi goodbye where Ruth clung (*davaq*) to her.

entries.title: Satan (ho satanas)
entries.summary: The name the New Testament gives the chief adversary, a role that had become a name.
entries.note: By the New Testament the role has become a name, and Revelation 12:9 works like a glossary entry, identifying the dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil, Satan, and the deceiver of the whole world as one figure. DDD's article (P. L. Day) treats the four Hebrew Bible passages with a celestial satan as most likely four separate beings, not one developing character. In Numbers 22:22-35 the satan is Yahweh's own messenger sent against Balaam, acting on Yahweh's orders. In Job 1-2 *hassatan* carries the article, which makes it a common noun ("the Accuser"), and the being is one of the sons of God at the council, testing whether Job's piety survives the loss of its reward without opposing God's rule outright. In Zechariah 3 the satan stands at the high priest Joshua's right hand to accuse him and is rebuked by Yahweh's messenger, a different figure again. Only in 1 Chronicles 21:1, without the article, does the word plausibly work as a proper name, and even there DDD notes that the earliest texts using Satan indisputably as a name (Assumption of Moses 10:1; Jubilees 23:29) come centuries later.
entries.dissent: Whether Revelation's identification is exegesis of Genesis 3 or a later synthesis read back into it is where serious readers part ways. Revelation 12:9 fuses the dragon, the ancient serpent of Genesis 3:1,14, the devil (slanderer), and Satan (adversary) into one figure, a deliberate synthesis that gathers every strand of cosmic opposition, from Eden on, into a single adversary. DDD goes further and calls the common claim that the Hebrew Bible shows a developing notion of Satan anachronistic on its own terms, since Satan by that name isn't in the Hebrew Bible at all and at least two of the four celestial-satan texts (Numbers 22 and Zechariah 3) plainly show different divine beings in different and even opposed roles.
sources: G. K. Beale and Sean M. McDonough, "Revelation," Commentary on the NT Use of the OT, 1125
C. Breytenbach and P. L. Day, DDD s.v. "Satan," 726-731

entries.title: The devil (diabolos)
entries.summary: The Greek word for slanderer, used interchangeably with Satan.
entries.note: The Greek word means slanderer, and it is what the Septuagint uses to translate *satan*. The English "devil" carries centuries of freight the Greek doesn't. In classical usage *diabolos* was an adjective, "slanderous," applied to gossips (the Pastorals still use it that way at 1 Timothy 3:11 and Titus 2:3), before it settled into a name. By the New Testament, *Satanas* and *Diabolos* name the same being and trade places freely (compare Mark 1:13 with Luke 4:2), and Hebrews 2:14 gives the devil "the power of death," a role Paul elsewhere assigns to Death and Hades as separate figures.
entries.secondTemple: DDD (G. J. Riley) traces the concept's growth after the exile to contact with Persian Zoroastrian dualism, which paired a good spirit and an evil one, each commanding armies of lesser spirits, locked in combat until a final judgment. Second Temple texts joined that framework to the older Near Eastern combat myth (Marduk against Tiamat, Baal against Yam and Mot) and to the Genesis 6 story of angels who fathered giants. In Jubilees 10:1-11 the leader of the fallen Watchers is identified as the devil, and the Testament of Solomon calls Beelzebul "the highest ranking angel in heaven" before his fall. On this reading the devil's rule over "the power of the air" (Ephesians 2:2) refers to the region where the demonic spirits of the drowned giants were believed trapped after the Flood.

entries.title: Beelzebul
entries.summary: The name Jesus's opponents used for the ruler of demons when they accused him.
entries.note: The charge against Jesus is that he casts out demons by their ruler, and his answer is the divided kingdom and the binding of the strong man. Cross-reference the Hebrew form at 2 Kings 1. DDD reads the name as a corruption story running opposite to what the spelling suggests. The god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consults is Ba'al Zebub, "Lord of the Flies," but Ugaritic texts use the title *zbl b'l ars*, "Prince, Lord of the Underworld," for Baal, and the philological consensus DDD follows (Dietrich and Loretz) reads the Hebrew as a deliberately mocking misspelling of the real epithet *zbl*, "Prince," with the Masoretic Text turning Baal the Prince into Baal the Fly on purpose. The New Testament's *Beelzeboul* keeps the older, correct form of the title, and "Beelzebub" in some English versions is a later correction back toward the Old Testament's insulting spelling.

entries.title: Belial / Beliar
entries.summary: A Hebrew word for worthlessness that hardened into a name for the enemy of God.
entries.note: In the Hebrew Bible a noun, "worthlessness" or "destruction," in phrases like "sons of Belial." In Paul a personal name set opposite Christ. DDD (S. D. Sperling) weighs several etymologies and settles on *beli* plus *ya'al*, "without worth," the construction behind Hebrew *al-mawet*, "deathlessness." What counts as a Belial deed in the Hebrew Bible is a list of specific crimes against the community: inciting idolatry (Deuteronomy 13:14), perjury (1 Kings 21:10,13), breaking hospitality (Judges 19:22), usurping a throne (2 Samuel 16:7-8), profaning a sanctuary by drunkenness (1 Samuel 1:13-17), and priests sexually exploiting the women who served at the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:12-22). In 2 Samuel 22:5, with Psalm 18:4-5, "torrents of Belial" runs parallel with "breakers of Death," likely a faded personification of death and chaos at this stage and not a full demonic name.
entries.secondTemple: The Qumran sectarian texts use Belial as the name of the opposing power throughout, bridging the two usages, and the Damascus Document is probably the earliest literary evidence of Belial as an unambiguous proper name. He is the commonest title at Qumran for the prince of darkness (angel of wickedness, ruler of this world, head of the demonic powers), and the War Scroll frames a struggle between Michael, Prince of Light, and Belial, Prince of Darkness, while keeping Belial subordinate to God ("who made Belial to corrupt, an angel of hatred"). DDD traces the dualism to Zoroastrianism, where the personified Drug, "Falsehood," opposes Asha, "Righteousness," a pairing the Pseudepigrapha echo by punning on Beliar as *beli 'or*, "without light." Paul's single New Testament use, "What harmony has Christ with Beliar?" (2 Corinthians 6:14-15), runs the same contrast of light and darkness. The Sibylline Oracles (3:63-64) later identify Beliar with a returning Nero, reading *Sebastenon* (from *Sebastos*, "Augustus") as a coded reference to the imperial line.

entries.title: Daimonion
entries.summary: The New Testament word for demon, borrowed from a Greek word that was morally neutral.
entries.note: In classical Greek a *daimon* is a morally neutral intermediate being, and the New Testament uses the word only negatively. Paul says what is sacrificed to idols is sacrificed to demons: the idol is nothing, and the thing behind it is not. DDD (G. J. Riley) traces the negative turn to the same Persian dualism that reshaped Satan and the devil. Once the gods of the nations were demoted, the Septuagint rendered those old, neutral pagan gods as *daimonia* outright, for Deuteronomy's *shedim* (LXX Deuteronomy 32:17), for Israel's neighbors' national gods in general (LXX Psalm 95:5, "all the gods of the nations are demons"), and for the god of fortune, Gad, at Isaiah 65:11 ("preparing a table for the demon"). Revelation keeps the equation. Idol worship is demon worship (Revelation 9:20), and fallen Babylon becomes "a dwelling place of demons" (Revelation 18:2), an image lifted from Isaiah's oracle of desert ruin against the literal Babylon.
entries.secondTemple: In the literature the New Testament writers actually read, the most common account of where demons came from is genealogy, not abstract dualism. A group of angels came down, married human women, and fathered a race of violent giants; the Flood killed the giants' bodies but not their spirits, and those disembodied spirits, "neither angelic nor human," became demons, trapped in the air and looking for human hosts. Justin Martyr cites the tradition explicitly (2 Apology 5, quoting Genesis 6:1-4). Paul's "power of the air" for the ruling demonic authority (Ephesians 2:2) reflects this cosmology.

entries.title: Shedim
entries.summary: A Hebrew word for the beings Israel sacrificed to, translated demons in Greek.
entries.note: Two occurrences, both about sacrificing to them, both calling them gods Israel didn't know, new arrivals their fathers never feared. The Septuagint renders the word *daimonia*, and that is how the two categories get connected. Heiser reads Deuteronomy 32:17 against its own context in 32:8-9, where the nations were divided among the sons of God at Babel: the *shedim* are those same allotted *elohim*, now indicted for abusing the guardianship they were given, spirit beings guarding foreign territory who must not be worshipped. The verse calls them *shedim* and *elohim* in the same breath, so it doesn't deny these beings exist; it denies Israel any right to worship them. Paul draws on this passage when he warns the Corinthians against fellowship with demons (1 Corinthians 10:20-21), which Heiser reads as evidence that Paul accepted the Deuteronomy 32 framework and didn't treat "demon" as empty pagan superstition.
entries.ane: Cognate with Akkadian *shedu*, which could mean either a protective spirit or a malevolent demon, with the plural leaning demonic. The Hebrew narrows the range more than it inverts it. Akkadian *shedu* named minor spirits tied to the dead that wouldn't normally receive sacrifice at all, and Deuteronomy 32:17 brands the *elohim* Israel sacrificed to as *shedim*, a deliberate demotion of beings that were minor divinities in their home setting.
sources: the LXX's *daimonia* for *shedim* is handled under "Demon," 235-239 (see Daimonion above)

entries.title: Se'irim
entries.summary: Goat demons, banned as objects of sacrifice and pictured haunting ruins.
entries.strong: H8163 (שָׂעִיר), 59 occ, nearly all ordinary goats, refs (the beings): Leviticus 17:7; 2 Chronicles 11:15; Isaiah 13:21; Isaiah 34:14
entries.note: Goat demons. Leviticus 17:7 forbids sacrificing to them, and nobody legislates that way about an animal. Isaiah puts them in ruined cities beside Lilith, dancing and calling to one another, while elsewhere they are plainly objects of worship. They were possibly pictured as mixed goat and demon beings standing for a wrecked, inhospitable world, and the Leviticus ban looks like real polemic, likely postexilic, against an actual cult. DDD (B. Janowski) notes that the LXX and later Jewish sources read the *se'irim* straightforwardly as demons: the Septuagint renders them *daimonia*, and Sifre on Leviticus 17:7 glosses the word as *shedim*. The Leviticus 17:7 ban sits one chapter after the Day of Atonement's scapegoat, where a live goat is sent out to Azazel in the wilderness (Leviticus 16:8-28), and Heiser reads the desert, more than the animal, as what both texts turn on, since the wilderness was understood as the place such beings lived.
sources: Heiser, *Unseen Realm*, 176-178 (on Azazel and the wilderness), note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Lilith
entries.summary: A night demon named once in Isaiah, in a list of creatures living in a ruin.
entries.note: One occurrence, in a list of desert creatures living in Edom's ruins. English versions render it night creature, screech owl, or night monster, and the Vulgate keeps *lamia*. The Talmudic Lilith material is specific and separate from the Ben Sira legend below. Eruvin 100b and Niddah 24b describe her as a demon with long hair and wings, Shabbat 151b warns a man not to sleep alone in a house in case Lilith finds him, and Bava Batra 73a makes her the daughter of Ahriman, the Zoroastrian opponent of Ohrmazd, the same Persian dualism that reshaped Satan and the devil in this period. None of these passages give her an origin as Adam's equal; that detail belongs to Ben Sira alone.
entries.ane: A Mesopotamian night demon attested well before Isaiah, with roots in the third millennium BC and in the Sumerian *lil*, "wind" or "spirit." The Babylonian Lilitu was a female spirit unable to bear children who poisoned infants from her breasts, associated with storm winds and with escaping houses through windows, and amulets and records show real popular fear of the *lilu*, a class of malevolent demons believed to attack infants and mothers in childbirth. DDD (M. Hutter) traces the figure to the Sumerian epic "Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld." Inanna plants a tree meaning to make a throne and a bed from it, but a snake nests in its roots, the Anzu bird settles in its crown, and the demon *ki-sikil-lil-la* makes her home in the trunk, so Gilgamesh has to cut the tree down to clear all three out. From the Middle Babylonian period on, Lilitu was merged with Lamashtu, the child-killing demon, and the ancient versions translate Isaiah 34:14 accordingly: the LXX has *onokentauros*, a donkey-centaur (echoing amulets that show Lamashtu standing on a donkey), Aquila transliterates "Lilith," and Symmachus and Jerome's Vulgate both give *lamia*, which Jerome's commentary glosses as an Erinys, a Greek fury.
entries.invented: Everything about Adam's first wife. That story comes from the Alphabet of Ben Sira, a medieval work that Eli Yassif, who produced its critical edition, places among the Jews of Abbasid Iraq in the ninth and tenth centuries. It was revised repeatedly, survives in more than a hundred manuscripts, and reached print only much later, at Constantinople and then Venice in 1544, and it isn't in Isaiah, the Talmud's Lilith passages, or any ancient Jewish source in that form. In it Lilith is created from the earth alongside Adam as his equal, refuses sexual subservience, speaks the divine Name, and flies off to the Sea of Reeds; when angels come to bring her back she says she would rather be a demon, and God makes Eve instead. It is a medieval recasting of the old Mesopotamian night demon as a figure of primordial rebellion.
sources: Christian M. M. Brady, "Lilith," Eerdmans Dictionary of the Bible, 810
