entries.title: The dragon
entries.summary: The beast of Revelation, identified there as the serpent, the devil and Satan all at once.
entries.strong: G1404 (δράκων), 13 occ in 12 verses, all in Revelation
entries.note: Thirteen occurrences, all in one book. Revelation 12:9 states the identification outright, and the tail that sweeps a third of the stars describes his following; it doesn't report a prehistoric fall. DDD (J. W. van Henten) reads Revelation 12 as combining at least two traditions: an older myth of a dragon-like god pursuing a pregnant goddess, the kind of combat myth also behind the Greek Python story and possibly echoing the Ugaritic story of Athtar trying to seize Baal's throne, and the Genesis 6 story of the fallen Watchers (1 Enoch 6-11). Outside Revelation, *drakon* in the Septuagint regularly translates ordinary Hebrew words for sea monsters and serpents (Leviathan at Isaiah 27:1, *tannin* in several places), and it is used against Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon to discredit the nations that oppressed Israel (Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2), the same rhetorical move Revelation makes against Rome.
entries.invented: "Satan took a third of the angels with him" as an event narrated in Scripture. Revelation 12:4 is a vision of the end, and the arithmetic is imported.

entries.title: The ancient serpent
entries.summary: The talking serpent of Eden, which the New Testament identifies with Satan though Genesis never does.
entries.note: Genesis 3 never names the serpent as Satan; the New Testament makes that identification, and the *nachash* wordplay (serpent, shining one, diviner) is what keeps the Genesis text from being a talking-animal story. Revelation 12:9 gives the figure two functions, slanderer and deceiver, which the Greek titles devil and Satan simply name, and both go back to what the serpent does in Genesis 3. DDD (R. S. Hendel) reads the Eden serpent as a trickster who blurs the lines between animal, human, and divine. He is classed as an animal (Genesis 3:1) yet has human speech, and unlike the humans he deceives he already knows what God confirms afterward, that eating the fruit won't kill them but will open their eyes (Genesis 3:22). DDD also flags that Genesis 3:20 calls the woman "mother of all living" right after the serpent scene, a formula that elsewhere in the ancient Near East is a goddess epithet, possibly a deliberate echo of the serpent's known association with a nude goddess in Canaanite iconography, probably Asherah. Even elsewhere in the New Testament the identification of serpent with Satan isn't automatic: John 3:14-15 uses the bronze serpent of Numbers 21 as a positive picture of Christ lifted up, the opposite value from Revelation's use of the same animal.
sources: G. K. Beale and Sean M. McDonough, "Revelation," Commentary on the NT Use of the OT, 1125

entries.title: The beast from the sea
entries.summary: The empire-beast of Revelation carrying the famous number.
entries.note: Daniel 7's four beasts collapsed into one, rising from the sea and given authority by the dragon. The number comes in 13:18 with a note that it takes wisdom. DDD's Behemoth article (B. F. Batto) says Revelation 13 is plainly informed by the Leviathan and Behemoth tradition: John's two beasts, one from the sea and one from the land, echo the same paired sea monster and land monster behind Job's Behemoth and Leviathan and, further back, Ugarit's sea dragon and El's calf Atik. Beale's commentary adds that first-century readers would have taken the sea beast as Rome, matching the standard Jewish reading of Daniel 7's fourth beast as Rome (attested repeatedly in Midrash Rabbah and the Babylonian Talmud), and that the beast's tie to the dragon marks it as transtemporal. Daniel 7:12 already has each defeated empire's life passed on to the next, so the power behind Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome is read as continuous and not as a series of unrelated evils.
entries.dissent: Nero *gematria*, a Domitianic setting, and futurist readings all have serious holders, and the number remains unresolved.
sources: G. K. Beale, *The Book of Revelation*, 684-685

entries.title: The beast from the earth / the false prophet
entries.summary: The second beast of Revelation, which looks like a lamb and talks like a dragon.
entries.note: Two horns like a lamb, and speaks like a dragon. Later called the false prophet, and that is the third figure in 16:13. Beale notes that Revelation introduces its four evil actors in a fixed order, the dragon (ch. 12), the sea beast (13:1-10), the land beast or false prophet (13:11-18), and Babylon (14:8), and narrates their defeat in reverse: Babylon falls first (chs. 17-18), then the beast and false prophet together (19:20), then the dragon (20:10). The reversal is a literary device marking one coordinated end and makes no claim about chronological sequence.
sources: G. K. Beale, *The Book of Revelation*

entries.title: The man of lawlessness
entries.summary: An end-times figure Paul describes and refuses to explain.
entries.note: Paul says his readers know what restrains him and doesn't say what it is, and nobody since has been able to say for certain. DDD (L. J. Lietaert Peerbolte) keeps one point straight: the word "antichrist" occurs only in the Johannine letters (1 John 2:18,22; 4:3; 2 John 7), never in 2 Thessalonians or Revelation, and the developed tradition of a single Antichrist familiar from later Christian writing isn't attested in full before Irenaeus, around AD 180. Paul's man of lawlessness is better described as a future anti-God figure than as the Antichrist of the later technical sense. John's letters use the word for the spirit of the writer's present opponents, already active and plural ("many antichrists have come," 1 John 2:18), not for one end-time individual, and 2 Thessalonians uses the Lawless One's still-future coming to argue that the end hasn't arrived, the opposite point from the one John and Revelation make with their villains. DDD also flags the Qumran pairing of Melchizedek and Melchiresha (4Q280-282; 4QAmram) as the nearest structural parallel outside the New Testament to a christ and antichrist typology.
sources: L. J. Lietaert Peerbolte, DDD s.v. "Antichrist," 62

entries.title: The ruler of this world
entries.summary: John's title for Satan, conceding real authority and announcing its end.
entries.note: Three times in John, each time in the setting of the cross, and each time as someone cast out or judged. The title concedes a real jurisdiction and announces its end in the same breath. DDD's Devil article (G. J. Riley) treats "ruler of this world" as one of a cluster of names covering the same ground: "the whole world lies in the power of the evil one" (1 John 5:19), and Satan claims to control "all the kingdoms of the world" when he offers them to Jesus (Luke 4:6). Early in the second century Ignatius of Antioch already uses a near-identical title, *archon tou aionos toutou*, "ruler of this age," as his usual name for Satan, more often than either "Satan" or "devil" (Ephesians 17:1; 19:1; Magnesians 1:2; Trallians 4:2; Romans 7:1; Philadelphians 6:2), so the title was standard early Christian vocabulary and not a Johannine one-off.

entries.title: The prince of the power of the air
entries.summary: Paul's title for the ruling evil power, with the air meaning contested territory overhead.
entries.note: *Archon* of the authority of the air. The cosmology behind it treats the lower heavens as contested territory, and the air here is more than atmosphere. DDD's Aion article confirms this was standard ancient cosmology, citing Philo (*De Gigantibus* 6) and 2 Enoch 29:4 for the air as the dwelling of evil spirits alongside Ephesians 2:2 itself. The Devil article gives the fuller mechanism: the spirits believed to occupy the air were the disembodied spirits of the giants drowned in the Flood, offspring of the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4, the tradition Eusebius later summarizes when he says Greek theologians assigned the atmosphere to demons (*Praeparatio Evangelica* 4.5.142).

entries.title: The god of this age
entries.summary: Paul calls the blinder of unbelievers a god, and translators have to decide what case to use.
entries.note: Paul calls him *theos*, and English translations lowercase it, a theological decision made in the typesetting. Greek has no case distinction between "a god" and "God," so capitalization is an English convention translators impose on their own reading of whom Paul means. The earliest manuscripts that preserve the verse, Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, write *theos* as a *nomen sacrum*, the abbreviated sacred form used for the true God elsewhere, which deepens the ambiguity, since the scribes may not have drawn the line modern translators draw. Most commentators and translations take the phrase as Satan; a minority reads it as God himself, since Paul elsewhere credits God with blinding unbelievers. DDD's Devil article (G. J. Riley) treats the title as one more name for the ruler of this world, whose kingdom of darkness takes in the whole world, the cosmos itself, and it reads 2 Corinthians 4:4 as naming how that rule works: the god of this age blinds minds to the light of the gospel.
sources: Brown, Twist, and Widder, *2 Corinthians*, Logos Research Commentaries

entries.title: Archai, exousiai, thronoi, kyriotetes
entries.summary: Paul's vocabulary for ranks of cosmic powers: rulers, authorities, thrones, dominions.
entries.note: Rulers, authorities, thrones, dominions. Colossians 1:16 has Christ creating them and Colossians 2:15 has him disarming them, both statements about the same class of being. DDD's articles on these terms (H. D. Betz on "Authorities," D. E. Aune on "Archai," M. de Jonge on "Thrones") add detail the New Testament never spells out. There is no Septuagint or pre-Christian Hellenistic precedent for *exousiai* as a class of heavenly beings; DDD traces the usage to Jewish apocalyptic (1 Enoch 61:10 lists "angels of the principalities" among the heavenly host), to magical papyri that pair the same terms in fixed formulas (*archai kai exousiai kai kosmokratores*, PGM 13.15), and possibly to early Gnostic sources. 1 Enoch 6:8 uses *archai* for twenty named fallen Watchers, each over ten lesser angels, an organization modeled on human military units of tens, fifties, and hundreds (compare Exodus 18:21,25). Colossians 1:16's list, thrones, dominions, rulers, powers, has no clear pre-Christian parallel as a class of angels; the closest is Testament of Levi 3:1-8, which puts "thrones and authorities" in the fourth of seven heavens, in a passage nobody can confirm predates Christian editing. DDD identifies 1 Peter 3:22 as the turning point. These powers were subjected to Christ after his resurrection and ascension, which implies they held real, God-given authority before that and turned hostile instead of being created evil.
entries.dissent: Whether these terms mean human political structures, spiritual beings, or both at once is a long-running argument with Wink on one side and Arnold on the other. Wink reads "powers" in the fullest sense, heavenly and earthly, divine and human, good and evil at once, an inner and outer unity of structure and spirit. Arnold answers that this is post-Enlightenment demythologizing out of step with first-century belief, and that Wink can't show from primary sources that people of the period didn't think of the powers as real entities. DDD adds a narrower dispute. In Romans 8:38 Paul pairs "angels" with "principalities" as though they were opposites, which Clement of Alexandria read as good angels against evil *archai*, while in 1 Corinthians 15:24 the *archai* are plainly hostile and marked for destruction along with "every authority and power." DDD concludes the terms are used loosely and more or less interchangeably across the Pauline letters without naming a fixed, ranked hierarchy, and that the rigid nine- or ten-tier angelic hierarchies (the longer recension of 2 Enoch 20:1, or Pseudo-Dionysius centuries later) are post-biblical systematizing that Paul and Colossians didn't have.
sources: John Anthony Dunne, "Principalities and Powers," *Lexham Bible Dictionary*
Heiser, "Principalities and Powers," Dictionary of Paul and His Letters, 860

entries.title: Stoicheia
entries.summary: A word meaning basic elements that Paul uses for something people can be enslaved to.
entries.note: Elements, basic principles, elemental spirits. In Hebrews it plainly means rudiments, and in Galatians it stands in parallel with beings that by nature are not gods, so the word does different jobs in the same canon. Colossians 2's two occurrences (2:8,20) sit among statements about spiritual beings, which is the strongest case for Arnold's hostile-powers reading, and the angels tied to the Law in Galatians 3:19-20 are the argument for carrying it into Galatians 4. DDD (L. J. Alderink) sets out the word's technical sense in Greek philosophy before Paul: Empedocles, Plato, and Aristotle used *stoicheia* for the four physical elements (earth, water, air, fire), the basic constituents of every object, and the Stoics built a cosmology on them in which the soul itself passes through the elements at death. On Galatians 4:3,9 DDD prefers the philosophical sense, since nothing in Paul's wording requires angels or demons, and it still lets the elements act as powers, the way Empedocles wrote of their power and Philo called them forces. On Colossians 2:8,20 it leaves the question open. Hebrews 5:12 it never reaches, and there the sense is plainly elementary teaching.
sources: John Anthony Dunne, "Principalities and Powers," *Lexham Bible Dictionary*
Arnold, "Returning to the Domain of the Powers: Stoicheia as Evil Spirits in Galatians 4:3, 9," *Novum Testamentum* 38:1 (1996): 55-76

entries.title: Legion
entries.summary: The demon who gives his name as a number, in the story that ends with the pigs.
entries.note: A name given as a number, in the Decapolis, across the lake, in the region the Enochic tradition ties to the territory of the giants' spirits. The pigs and the drowning are the scene; the geography carries the argument.
entries.secondTemple: 1 Enoch 15:8-12 explains demons as the disembodied spirits of the dead giants, the framework Mark's audience would have had. At death the giants' spirits come out of their bodies to plague humankind, and they are set apart from heavenly spirits whose proper home is heaven. The geography sharpens it. Bashan's ancient boundaries match the area where Jesus performs this exorcism, and Second Temple Jews understood the demons there as Watcher-spirits released at the death of the ancient Nephilim and Rephaim; the Dead Sea Scrolls call them "bastard spirits," the hybrid offspring of Genesis 6:1-4. In Jubilees 10, Mastema, leader of the evil spirits, bargains to keep a tenth of the demons active on earth under his command ("if none of them is left for me I shall not be able to exercise the authority of my will among humankind"), God grants it, and the other nine-tenths go to the place of judgment, a different Second Temple accounting of the problem Legion embodies. This Enoch and Jubilees reading of Genesis 6:1-4 became the standard lens carried into the New Testament period, and a recent ICC commentary on 1 Peter traces the same Watcher framework through the "spirits in prison" of 1 Peter 3:19-20, reading them against this Second Temple material instead of as an isolated image.
entries.dissent: DDD's Legion article (H. D. Betz) doesn't use the giants'-spirits framework at all and reads the name through anti-Roman polemic. A legion was the largest unit of the Roman army, and the story has Legion's cohorts drowned along with two thousand pigs, an image DDD calls an obvious, deliberate insult to the occupation. DDD also traces a later Jewish magical tradition in the Testament of Solomon (11:1-6), where the demon reveals that his true name isn't Legion but "the Lion-Shaped Demon, an Arab by descent," with Legion describing his function, "the name for all demons which are under me." The Gospel text supports the demonological reading without ruling out the political one DDD favors.

entries.title: Abaddon / Apollyon
entries.summary: A word for the place of destruction that Revelation turns into an angel over the abyss.
entries.strong: G3, 1 occ; G623, 1 occ; Hebrew *abaddon* in Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11
entries.note: Revelation gives both the Hebrew and the Greek, the angel of the abyss and king of the locusts, and does that nowhere else at this length. In the Old Testament the word names a place, paired with Sheol. DDD (M. Hutter) is careful about how thin the demonic reading is in the Hebrew Bible. In most of its six Old Testament occurrences Abaddon is simply a place, "place of destruction," with no personification (Job 31:12 is purely topographical). DDD makes Job 28:22 the turning point, where Abaddon and Death together are personified beings who "hear" a report, with a slighter hint in Proverbs 27:20, where Abaddon is never satisfied. Apocalyptic tradition then turns the place into an angel: Apocalypse of Zephaniah 10:3 and 1 Enoch 20:2 both feature an angel over the underworld comparable to Revelation's Abaddon. The Greek name Apollyon is a translation and also a pun, since ancient readers already connected *apollymi*, "destroy," with Apollo, a god of plague and destruction as early as Aeschylus, so John's readers likely heard a jab at Apollo behind the angel's Greek name.
sources: M. Hutter, DDD s.v. "Abaddon," 1, note-to-build: both currently `kind: person`

entries.title: Death and Hades
entries.summary: Death and the grave, treated in Revelation as figures who ride and get thrown into fire.
entries.note: Given a horse to ride and then thrown into the lake of fire, a strange fate for an abstraction. Paul calls death the last enemy to be destroyed. DDD (J. N. Bremmer) is frank about how little of the Greek god survives in the Bible's usage. Hades in Greek myth is a specific and nearly cultless deity (only Elis worshipped him in a temple), best known for abducting Persephone, and none of that mythology carries over. In the Septuagint *Hades* occurs 111 times, almost always as the standard translation of Sheol, and DDD explains the personified Death that rides a horse or is thrown into the lake of fire (1 Corinthians 15:55 in some manuscripts; Revelation 6:8; 20:13-14) as a continuation of the Old Testament's own personification of Death, Mot, more than any trace of the Greek god.

entries.title: The four angels of the Euphrates
entries.summary: Angels tied up at a river and released on schedule to kill.
entries.note: Bound at the great river and released at an appointed hour to kill a third of mankind, bound like the Watchers and released on a schedule set elsewhere. DDD's Euphrates article (K. van der Toorn) places this in a real ancient Near Eastern cosmology. In Mesopotamian myth the Euphrates is a branch of the primeval cosmic river marking the boundary between the world of the living and the netherworld, the same function it has in Revelation. DDD reads Revelation 9:14 and 16:12 as two expressions of one idea. In 9:14 the river is the boundary between the living and the dead, with four death-dealing angels held there, and in 16:12 its drying up opens a road for "the kings from the east," a phrase DDD suggests may mean rulers of the underworld as well as earthly armies. DDD also points to a close Jewish apocalyptic parallel. In 2 Esdras 13:39-47 the exiled ten tribes cross the narrows of the Euphrates into a far country called Arzareth, "Other Land," and at the end of time "the Most High will stop the channels of the river again" so they can cross back, the same picture of the river as passage to and from the realm of the dead.
sources: K. van der Toorn, DDD s.v. "Euphrates," 314-315 ---

entries.title: Lucifer
entries.summary: Not a name and not Satan: a Latin word for the morning star, used of a Babylonian king.
entries.note: *Helel ben-shahar*, "shining one, son of Dawn." It isn't a name, it isn't in the Hebrew as one, and the passage isn't about Satan. The Vulgate's *lucifer* is a Latin common noun for the morning star, and capitalizing it into a proper name is an accident of English. The "stars of God" the figure means to rise above (Isaiah 14:13) is the phrase Job 38:7 uses for the sons of God at creation. No extant ancient Near Eastern text matches Helel's story point for point, including the closest proposed parallel, the Ugaritic god Athtar's failed bid for Baal's throne: Athtar isn't called Shahar's son, isn't thrown down, and the episode isn't framed as rebellion (Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on Isaiah 14:12-13).
entries.dissent: That the passages carry a cosmic-rebel backdrop is defensible, and Heiser defends it. His case (*Unseen Realm*, ch. 11, "Like the Most High?") reads Isaiah 14:12-15 through the same divine-council vocabulary as Ezekiel 28, "stars of God," "mount of assembly," Zaphon, calls the episode an attempted coup in the divine council, and treats Helel as a divine throne-guardian type, parallel in structure to the *nachash* of Genesis 3 and not identical with it. That is a different claim from "this is Satan's biography," and the entry keeps them apart.
entries.invented: The whole biography, heaven's worship leader, pride, and the fall, built on Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28, two *mashal* poems addressed by name to the king of Babylon and the prince of Tyre. Isaiah 14 is openly a taunt song, a sarcastic funeral lament, and the king's offense in the poem is "you have destroyed your land and killed your people," so the cosmic-ambition reading is imported. Jerome's Vulgate rendered *helel* with the Latin word for Venus as morning star, "light-bearer," and the shift from common noun to proper name followed Tertullian's and Origen's identification of the verse with Satan; by the KJV the reading was settled enough that "Lucifer" stayed in the English text. The retrojection adds a second anachronism. "Satan" doesn't become a personal name for a chief of demons until roughly the second century BC, so Isaiah's first audience had no Satan to identify Helel with (Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on Ezekiel 28:16-17).
sources: John H. Walton and J. Harvey Walton, *Demons and Spirits in Biblical Theology*, 218-219
Elwell & Beitzel, "Lucifer," Baker Encyclopedia of the Bible, 2:1360
Page, "The Astral Revolt," PhD diss., Harvard, 1990
Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on Isaiah 14:12-13 and Ezekiel 28:16-17
W. G. E. Watson, DDD s.v. "Helel," 392-393, note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Satan the worship leader
entries.summary: The belief that Satan ran music in heaven, built on one obscure verse about stone settings.
entries.note: The KJV's "tabrets" and "pipes," read as a musical office in heaven. The Hebrew is obscure and concerns settings for stones; the instrument reading is one option among several, and it carries no job description with it. One older critical reading separates "and gold" from the preceding list of stones and renders the line as the workmanship of settings and grooves for gems, with no music at all, so the meaning of the text is uncertain and not settled in the instruments' favor. The list of precious stones (v. 13) parallels the twelve stones of the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-20; 39:10-13), not an inventory of instruments. DDD and Walton both identify the figure beneath the oracle as Melqart, patron god of Tyre. The prince of Tyre claims equality with him (Ezekiel 28:2), and the precious stones (v. 12), the fire he walks among (v. 14), and the fire that consumes him (v. 18) echo Melqart's cult, including Nonnos of Panopolis's description of the god's star-studded robe and the Phoenician tradition of Melqart burned and buried in Tyre (DDD s.v. "Melqart," 563-564; Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on Ezekiel 28:2,12-14). Reading this as Satan's biography has no textual warrant beyond surface imagery. Satan is never called a cherub or paired with one anywhere in Scripture, and "Satan" doesn't exist as a personal name for a chief of demons until roughly the second century BC, centuries after Ezekiel. Calvin rejected the same Satan reading of Isaiah 14 outright (Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on Ezekiel 28:16-17).
sources: A. B. Davidson, *The Book of the Prophet Ezekiel*, Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges, 206
Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on Ezekiel 28:2,12-14,16-17

entries.title: Mammon
entries.summary: An Aramaic word for money that Jesus personified, later mistaken for a demon.
entries.note: An Aramaic word, *mamona*, for wealth or property, probably from the root *'mn*, "that in which one trusts." Jesus personifies it as a rival master, which is rhetoric and not demonology: "No servant can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and money" (Luke 16:13). The Greek plays on the root two verses earlier: "If you have not been faithful (*pistoi*) in the unrighteous mammon, who will entrust (*pisteusei*) to you the true riches?" (Luke 16:11). The demon of greed isn't purely a medieval invention, either. Some later Christian sources already personify Mamonas as a demon on the strength of Luke 16:13 setting him against God as a rival *kyrios*, well before Milton and the occult lists gave the figure a face and a rank (DDD s.v. "Mammon," 542).
sources: DDD s.v. "Mammon," 542, note-to-build: missing from entities.json

entries.title: Jehovah
entries.summary: Not a name anyone in the Bible used, but a misreading of God's name produced centuries later.
entries.note: No one in Scripture used this name. It is the consonants of YHWH read with the vowels of *adonai*, a reading aid for a name not to be pronounced, taken for a word by sixteenth-century Christian Hebraists. DDD calls it exactly that, the Masoretic form: the consonants of one word carrying the vowels of another. The scholarly "Yahweh" is itself a reconstruction, resting on early Greek transliterations of the name in Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* 5.6.34.5) and Epiphanius of Salamis (*Adv. Haer.* 1.3.40.5), and not on any form written or vocalized that way in the Hebrew text.

entries.title: The third of the angels
entries.summary: The claim that a third of the angels fell with Satan, which no passage actually reports.
entries.note: The one-third comes from the dragon's tail sweeping the stars in a vision of the end, and no passage anywhere in Scripture narrates a prehistoric angelic rebellion with a casualty count. Stars stand for angelic beings elsewhere in Scripture (Judges 5:20; Daniel 8:10; 12:3; Revelation 1:20), so the swept stars of Revelation 12:4 belong to the same symbolic idiom and aren't a literal headcount. Origen already admitted the church had no settled teaching on how the demons originated, and he traced one competing view, that the devil "induced many of the angels to fall away with him" after his own apostasy, back to this verse (*De Principiis* pref. 6; compare Tatian, *Oratio ad Graecos* 20). DDD takes this as evidence that the tradition reasoned backward from Revelation 12:4 and wasn't reporting a remembered event (DDD s.v. "Demon," 235-239).
sources: Heiser, *Unseen Realm*, on the fall traditions

entries.title: Lilith, Adam's first wife
entries.summary: A medieval story, not a biblical one.
entries.note: See the Lilith entry. The story is medieval, from the Alphabet of Ben Sira (ninth or tenth century, Abbasid Iraq, per Yassif), and the two-creation-accounts argument now attached to it is a modern addition. The Talmud already knows Lilith as a night demon centuries before that legend (Eruvin 100b; Niddah 24b; Shabbat 151b), and Bava Batra 73a makes her the daughter of Ahriman, the Zoroastrian adversary. Isaiah 34:14 is her only biblical mention, and even that is disputed in translation: the LXX renders her *onokentauros*, "donkey-centaur," Aquila transliterates the name, and Symmachus and Jerome's Vulgate both give *lamia* (DDD s.v. "Lilith," 520-521).

entries.title: The Nephilim as extraterrestrials
entries.summary: The claim that the giants of Genesis were aliens, which rests on mistranslated Sumerian.
entries.note: Assyriologists reject Sitchin's reading of the Sumerian texts on lexical grounds, not theological ones. The biblical material says less than the fringe claims and more than the flattened reading allows, and the entry says both. Genesis 6:1-4 claims that the sons of God, read as divine beings in line with the heavenly council elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible (Psalms 29:1; 82:6; 89:6; Job 1-2; 1 Kings 22:19-22; Isaiah 6:1-8), married human women and produced the Nephilim, whom the LXX and Vulgate both render "giants" (*gigantes*); the Nephilim of Numbers 13:33, after the Flood, lose the semi-divine overtones and read as an ordinary, if exaggerated, ancient people of great size (DDD s.v. "Nephilim," 618-619). Heiser frames Genesis 6:1-4 as a deliberate polemic against the Mesopotamian apkallu tradition of antediluvian divine sages, turning that story over point by point to warn Israel off it, and not a garbled memory of alien visitors (*Reversing Hermon*, ch. 1, 3). None of this is extraterrestrial contact, and none of it is merely folklore.
sources: Michael S. Heiser, "The Myth of a Sumerian 12th Planet: 'Nibiru' According to the Cuneiform Sources" (self-published paper, sitchiniswrong.com, written early 2003 while he was a PhD candidate at Wisconsin-Madison
Heiser, "The Myth of a 12th Planet in Sumero-Mesopotamian Astronomy: A Study of Cylinder Seal VA 243" (self-published paper, sitchiniswrong.com)
*Chicago Assyrian Dictionary* N/2, 145-147, s.v. *neberu* (the lexical evidence Heiser's paper rests on, as he cites it)
B. Landsberger and J. V. Kinnier Wilson, "The Fifth Tablet of Enuma Elish," *JNES* 20 (1961): 172ff.

entries.title: The ghost of Samuel
entries.summary: The dead prophet called up by a medium, in a scene that terrifies the medium herself.
entries.note: The text says Samuel, the medium is terrified by what actually comes up, and the message delivered is accurate. The demonic-impersonation reading is a later harmonization and not what the narrator reports. The medium describes what she sees as *'elohim*, literally "a god," coming up out of the earth (1 Samuel 28:13), and DDD treats the episode as a plain case of Israelite necromancy in which even the effectiveness of the conjuring is left intact by the editor (DDD s.v. "Dead," 223). The ritual follows the standard ancient Near Eastern pattern for raising the dead through a pit, and nothing in the text says the woman was possessed or spoke in a trance. She conjures the spirit and reports what she sees and hears, which is not a medium in the modern channeling sense (Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on 1 Samuel 28:7-11). Saul recognizes Samuel by his prophet's robe (1 Samuel 28:14).
sources: Walton, IVP Bible Background Commentary: OT, on 1 Samuel 28:3-14

entries.title: Dagon the fish god
entries.summary: The belief that the Philistine god was part fish, which comes from medieval wordplay.
entries.note: See the Dagon entry. The fish etymology and the mermaid iconography both descend from medieval commentary on a Hebrew pun, and the etymology of Dagan or Dagon is unresolved, not settled toward "fish." DDD calls the fish, grain, and storm etymologies all equally dubious and treats the fish reading as a secondary folk etymology. The fish tradition goes back to a specific textual crux. At 1 Samuel 5:4 the Masoretic Text's obscure *raq dagon nish'ar 'alayw*, "only Dagon was left on him," was emended by Wellhausen to *dago*, "his fish part," a reading anticipated by Jerome (who glosses the name *dag 'on*, "fish of sorrow") and later Jewish tradition, and BHS has now dropped the emendation. Dagan was a major Mesopotamian and West Semitic god well before the Philistines adopted him, attested from the third millennium BC at Ebla and Mari and identified at Ugarit as the father of Baal; the Philistines are the ones who shift the vowel from Dagan to Dagon.

entries.title: Easter from Ishtar
entries.summary: The claim that Easter is named after a Babylonian goddess, which fails as word history.
entries.note: A claim about etymology, not about a being, and it fails as etymology. The English word descends from a spring month name, and most languages call the feast some form of *Pascha*. The chain runs through Hislop's *The Two Babylons*, and it fails a second way as well: DDD confirms that Ishtar is never named as a deity anywhere in the Bible, and the only proposed biblical traces are the name Esther (a disputed derivation) and a possible allusion in the title Queen of Heaven (Jeremiah 7:18; 44:17-19,25) (DDD s.v. "Ishtar," 452-455). Heiser, Walton, and DDD's Dagan, Astarte, and Ishtar articles never connect Easter to Ishtar at all, and nothing in the local library supports the popular chain.
sources: Bede, *De temporum ratione*, on the month name
